<!-- chapter: higgsfield/platform-mastery.md -->
# Higgsfield Platform Mastery

## The model roster (what to use when)

Higgsfield is model-agnostic — it hosts many engines under one credit pool. Third-party model guides rank them this way (tiers: Free / Low 0.1–2 credits / Mid 2–10 / Premium 10+):

| Need | Model | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| Top-tier cinematic video + native audio | Kling 3.0 | Premium |
| Epic scale / spectacle | Kling 3.0 | Premium |
| Nature / landscapes + reference images | Veo 3.1 | Premium |
| Artistic / stylized video | Wan 2.6 | Mid |
| Fast iteration | Seedance 2.0 Pro | Mid |
| VFX / fluid motion | Minimax Hailuo 2.3 | Mid |
| Budget-friendly video | Kling 2.5 Turbo / Higgsfield DoP Lite | Free–Low |

Image side: Soul 2.0 (fashion/aesthetic, free), Soul Cinema (cinematic stills with film grain and era-aware styling), Nano Banana Pro (photorealistic, low cost), Soul Cast (AI actor generation).

**Key insight:** a clip made through Higgsfield on the Kling engine is a Kling clip — what differs is how you buy it (shared credit pool) and what you can steer (presets vs raw prompt control). Going to Kling directly exposes controls Higgsfield's preset UI hides: end-frame pinning, multi-reference `elements`, multi-prompt shots, 3–15s durations.

## Cinema Studio — the filmmaking layer

Cinema Studio is Higgsfield's director-mode workspace:

- **Camera movement controls:** static, handheld, zoom, pan, dolly, orbit and more — several moves can be stacked in one shot
- **Genre settings:** Action, Epic, Drama, Comedy, Horror — the whole scene follows the genre's look and pacing
- **Era selection:** regrade to look like the 1960s, 1980s, 1990s, or today
- **AI Cast:** build custom AI actors with chosen look, outfit, era, personality
- **Scene building:** place locations and props, shape the frame
- **Emotions:** choose what each character shows
- **Color grading:** fine-tune color, temperature, contrast, presets
- **Multiple references:** upload many reference images to guide generation
- **Real-time co-directing:** invite teammates onto one project
- **AI assistant:** help with camera angles, lighting, prompts, script-to-shot breakdowns

It isn't tied to one model — pick the best engine per shot.

## Generation controls that matter

- **Start frame:** upload or generate the opening image; the clip grows from it. This is the single biggest quality lever.
- **End frame** (where supported): pin exactly where a camera move finishes — turns drift into intention.
- **Camera movement presets:** faster than prompt engineering; pick the move, don't describe it.
- **Duration:** longer clips cost more and drift more. Short, locked shots chain better than long wandering ones.
- **Aspect ratio:** match your delivery format from the first generation, never crop later.

## Turbo vs Standard thinking

- **Standard / Premium models (Kling 3.0 etc.):** hero shots — faces, dialogue, key story beats.
- **Turbo / Lite models:** iteration, B-roll, establishers, tests. Draft cheap, render the winners expensive.
- **One clip at a time, quality-gated:** a failed clip never chains. Re-prompt, don't hope.

## Reliability rules

1. Never spend credits on a guess — pre-check the prompt against the checklists in `prompt-engineering.md`.
2. Failed/NSFW generations aren't billed on the API path; verify billing behavior in the app before a big batch.
3. Credits reset each billing cycle and don't roll over — plan usage so paid credits don't evaporate.
4. Higgsfield open-sourced three of its own AI films with every prompt, camera setting, and asset published — mine those before inventing your own pipeline.

## Sources

- https://www.thehypemagazine.com/2026/10/09/what-is-higgsfield-ai-uses-features-pricing/

<!-- chapter: higgsfield/prompt-engineering.md -->
# Higgsfield Prompt Engineering

## The anatomy of a prompt that works

Treat the prompt as a directing system, not a description. Every generation should specify, in order:

1. **Subject** — who/what, locked identity
2. **Micro-action** — one believable action, not three
3. **Environment** — where, with subtle motion in it
4. **Camera behavior** — one intentional move (see below)
5. **Lighting design** — explicit and physical ("golden-hour side light, long shadows")
6. **Visual style** — cinematic, anamorphic, film grain, era
7. **Emotional tone** — the feeling of the shot
8. **Physics & motion details** — how things move (cloth in breeze, steam rising)
9. **Rendering quality modifiers** — 4K, shallow depth of field, stable architecture

Missing layers = randomness. "Slow dolly push-in" beats "zoom in." Explicit lighting beats "nice lighting."

## Camera phrasing that the models obey

- **Push-in / reveal:** "the camera slowly dollies toward the subject with smooth stabilized movement"
- **Pull-back / scale:** "the camera slowly pulls backward, gradually revealing the enormous environment surrounding the subject"
- **Orbit:** "camera orbits 360° around the subject"
- **Pan:** "slow camera pan across the scene"
- **Stacked moves:** Higgsfield's Cinema Studio supports several moves in one shot — but one motivated move beats two unmotivated ones.

Rule: every movement needs a purpose. Ask what the move reveals or withholds.

## The Soul ID prompting rule

When a Soul ID character is active, **do not re-describe the face or core features** — the Soul ID handles that. Describe only what changes: wardrobe, setting, action, expression, camera, light, style.

Good: "The Soul ID character now wears a formal black suit, standing at a podium addressing a conference room. Camera: dolly in toward her face. Style: cinematic, cool corporate lighting."

## The exclusion block

Always exclude what breaks cinematic output: morphing faces, extra limbs, melting hands, warping architecture, flicker, watermark-like artifacts, text in frame (unless wanted). Put it in every prompt, not just the risky ones.

## Per-shot discipline

- One shot = one fully self-contained prompt. Restate the full premise every time — the model has no memory of your last clip.
- Don't ask for too many actions in five seconds. One action per clip.
- Keep the frame uncrowded. Fewer subjects = fewer failure modes.
- Image-to-video (start frame first) beats text-to-video for control. Generate the still, approve it, then animate.

## Common failure modes and fixes

| Failure | Fix |
|---|---|
| Face morphs mid-shot | Shorter clip; Soul ID or reference image; re-generate from a locked start frame |
| Melting hands | Keep hands out of frame or still; exclude "deformed hands"; crop in post |
| Camera drift (unmotivated) | Pin an end frame; name one explicit camera move; shorten duration |
| Identity drift across shots | Soul ID; same seed discipline; approved-frame library as start frames |
| Flicker / texture boil | Regenerate; avoid overly busy backgrounds; stabilize in post |
| Plasticky faces in wide shots | Shoot closer; composite a close-shot face in post |

<!-- chapter: higgsfield/soul-id-deep-dive.md -->
# Soul ID Deep Dive

## What it is

Soul ID is Higgsfield's character-consistency layer: train it once on photos of one person and the same face appears across every generation — any style, pose, lighting, or angle. It's the equivalent of casting the same actor for the entire film.

A reference image anchors a single generation but drifts across many. Soul ID trains a reusable identity once and holds it.

## How to train (official requirements)

From Higgsfield's help center:

1. Open higgsfield.ai → **Soul** → **Train new character**
2. **Prepare photos:** 20 or more of the same person (up to 80 supported)
   - High-quality and well-lit
   - Face from different angles and expressions
   - No sunglasses, no heavy shadows, no cropped faces
   - Include at least one full-height photo
   - Recent photos for the most accurate likeness
   - Only your own face or someone who gave permission
3. Upload and start training — takes a few minutes
4. Name the character
5. Generate — select it in the **Character** tab

## Using it in production

- **Soul ID locks identity; everything else follows your prompt.** Wardrobe, setting, action, camera, light — all prompt-driven.
- **Prompting rule:** never re-describe the face. Describe only what changes from the base character.
- **Works across the Soul family** (Soul 2.0, Soul Cinema, Cinema Studio, Marketing Studio, supported video models).
- **Caveat:** Soul IDs are tied to the model they were trained in — a character trained in Soul 2.0 may need retraining for Soul Cinema. Verify before a big shoot.

## When to use it / when to skip it

Use: multi-shot sequences, short films with a recurring protagonist, series content, AI influencers, brand mascots, action sequences needing the same hero.

Skip: single one-off shots (overkill), or when you want maximum creative variation — consistency limits style range.

## Identity drift: causes and fixes

- **Drift across many generations:** re-anchor with the trained Soul ID selected; don't fall back to per-generation reference uploads.
- **Wide-shot face collapse:** faces go plasticky at distance — shoot closer, or composite a close-shot face in post.
- **Feature drift:** keep a character sheet (front, 3/4, side reference) and use it as the reference image when drift appears.
- **Never fabricate identity frames.** The trained Soul ID is the identity authority — every clip's face must trace back to it, never to an invented start frame.

## Sources
- https://higgsfield.ai/creator-hub/help-center/ai-models/how-do-i-create-and-use-a-soul-id-character

<!-- chapter: higgsfield/competition-entry-craft.md -->
# Competition-entry craft

Judged AI-film competitions are a production teacher, not a lottery ticket. This chapter is about what their constraints and judging criteria teach you about making professional work — whether or not you ever enter one.

## Why competitions are worth studying

A competition hands you three things most productions never get:

1. **Hard constraints** — runtime limits, delivery specs, content rules. Constraints are a forcing function for craft: every decision the rules make for you is a decision you can't get wrong.
2. **A published quality bar** — judging criteria tell you exactly what experienced eyes score: directing, craft, sound, originality. That's a checklist you can aim any film at.
3. **A body of judged work** — winning entries are public. Shot-by-shot teardowns of what placed are the cheapest film school available (see `case-studies/competition-teardowns.md`).

## The constraint set that shapes production

Real competition rulebooks converge on the same production discipline. Treat each as a standing habit:

- **Runtime discipline.** Competitions cap entries at a few minutes. The craft lesson: a 3-minute film that lands beats a 10-minute film that drifts. Budget your runtime like your credits — every shot must earn its seconds.
- **Delivery specs are real.** Watermarks, packshots, aspect ratios, masters. The craft lesson: professional delivery is a package, not a file. Build your delivery checklist before you lock picture (see `skills/delivery/`).
- **Rights hygiene.** Competition rules typically require AI-generated music/voice/sound with rights held by the creator. The craft lesson: clear every asset's rights at generation time, not at delivery. Keep the receipts in your asset registry.
- **Likeness safety.** "No real person's face or voice" is a common rule — not even your own. The craft lesson: never build a film on likeness you can't clear. Synthetic characters and Soul IDs are the safe default.
- **Small teams, async.** Winning entries are routinely made by 2–4 people across time zones. The craft lesson: a tight team with a shared asset registry beats a large team with a group chat.

## What juries actually reward

Across Runway AIFF, Project Odyssey, Reply AIFF, the Higgsfield Action Contest, and MIT's hackathon, judges reward the same things: **story over spectacle, authorial intent, character/POV discipline, originality, sound design, and polish as the floor.** They punish: visible morphing/inconsistency, generic "AI slop," tech demos without narrative, and AI that pulls focus from the story.

Distilled: narrative cohesion + committed POV + intentional AI use + pro-grade sound + consistent visuals. Originality is the tiebreaker; polish is the entry ticket.

Direct for that jury — story, cinematography, craft — not for the AI-tools audience. The film that wins is the one that would work if nobody knew how it was made.

## Craft patterns from judged work

Higgsfield's Action Contest (8,752 submissions, 139 countries) shows what experienced filmmakers do with AI:

- **"GRANDMA vs WASP"** — Muhannad Nassar & Simon Meyer. The makers never met in person; fully async workflow across time zones. *Lesson:* decentralized production works when the asset pipeline is disciplined.
- **"CUPID"** — Shestak Nikolay, actor/filmmaker. Concepts that would need prohibitive traditional budgets. *Lesson:* AI used for impossible scale, not novelty.
- **"SCRATCH"** — Ash & Aram Gevorkyan, made in **five days**. Director + 3D/VFX generalist duo; production value audiences mistook for a studio trailer. *Lesson:* a tight team with real craft compresses schedules AI can't compress alone.

Pattern: experienced filmmakers using AI for impossible scale, tight teams, real craft — not tech demos.

## Study the open-sourced winners

Higgsfield open-sourced three of its own AI films with every prompt, camera setting, and asset published. Before spending a credit, study a complete production's actual prompts and settings — it's the closest thing to sitting in someone else's edit bay.

## Competition-entry delivery checklist

- [ ] Final cut locked to the runtime cap, master to spec (aspect, watermark/packshot if required)
- [ ] All music/voice/sound rights cleared and documented in the asset registry
- [ ] No uncleared likeness anywhere in the film
- [ ] Credits and key art treated as craft, not an afterthought
- [ ] Team roles and handoffs defined before production starts

## Sources
- https://higgsfield.ai/blog/higgsfield-global-film-festival
- https://aivideosensei.com/guides/higgsfield-global-film-festival-guide
- https://medium.com/@sanwsman7/i-didnt-believe-ai-could-make-a-real-film-until-i-tried-higgsfield-ai-de0b4ee68072

<!-- chapter: field/2026-developments.md -->
# 2026: The Year AI Film Went Long-Form

The state of the field as of October 2026. This chapter is a dated snapshot, not doctrine: model versions, prices, and festival rules move fast. Every claim below carries its source; single-sourced items are flagged. For the machine-readable model data, see `api/v1/models.json` (per-model `last_verified`, `status`, `what_changed`, `sources`).

## The headline: a fully AI-generated feature premiered at a major festival

On June 10, 2026, Tribeca premiered *Dreams of Violets* — a 75-minute docudrama by Fountain 0 (written/directed/produced by Ash Koosha, co-produced by Pooya Koosha). Fountain 0 describes it as the first feature-length live-action film completely generated by AI to be accepted to a major festival. The film is a fictionalized dramatization of the January 2026 Iranian protests: five strangers hiding in a dead-end Tehran alley at dawn, a violent soldier who discovers them, and Amir — a 10-year-old boy with cerebral palsy — watching from a window and deciding to act. Every image and person in it was AI-generated; the story was built from journalistic reports, photographs, and eyewitness accounts.

The documented production stack (businesswire.com and consequence.net, May 27, 2026):

- **Video generation:** Kling AI
- **Language editing:** Anthropic Claude
- **Research and imagery:** Google Gemini + Nano Banana
- **Blocking and frame accuracy:** Fountain 0's own technology

The headline numbers: made in three months for **~$2,000** (Fountain 0 executive chairman Tom Rogers cited "incredibly efficient cost management techniques"). Tribeca co-founder Jane Rosenthal endorsed the selection on the strength of "the emotional immediacy and urgency of the story itself." Ash Koosha addressed the ethics directly: a film about people who actually died "raises difficult questions," he said — his answer was that silence and forgetting were worse, and "the dead deserve to be witnessed." The film later became rentable on Fountain 0's own site (Wikipedia, *Dreams of Violets*).

What this actually proves: a feature can now be *produced* for the price of a used laptop — but the film was still human-directed end to end (written, directed, produced by the Koosha brothers, with a language-editing pass). It is a production-cost revolution, not an authorship one. A shot-by-shot teardown of its documented craft is in `api/v1/teardowns.json` ("Dreams of Violets").

## The 2026 model field: 4K + native audio is the baseline

By October 2026 the field had consolidated around 4K output and native audio as table stakes. The current map (sources: creativeainews.com, Sept 2026; versely.studio, Oct 1, 2026; blog.laozhang.ai, Sept 30, 2026):

- **Kling 3.0** (Kuaishou, launched Feb 4, 2026) — the current GA flagship: native 4K 60fps, 16-bit HDR, "Omni Native Audio." API ~$0.084–$0.168/s (720p/1080p), 4K $0.42/s; plans $10–$37/mo.
- **Kling 4.0** (Kuaishou) — **announced September 28, 2026; not generally available.** Kling 4.0 Flash opened in limited early access for Ultra Yearly subscribers the same day; the full model is scheduled for October 2026 but had not launched as of early October. Kling 3.0 remains the model you can actually use today. Multiple outlets covered the announcement (techtimes.com, Sept 30; Pandaily via aiaffairs.com, Sept 29; curatedai.net); one field roundup (versely.studio, Oct 1) called 4.0 "unannounced" — that was wrong or stale; the announcement is multi-sourced. **Leak-level flag (Oct 11, 2026):** the "30-second single-pass" spec is preview-leak level — GPTProto (medium.com/@gptproto.team) explicitly cautions it is unverified. Do not present 4.0 specs as confirmed. Note: Kling 4K is a **3.0** feature (native 4K added April 23, 2026), not a 4.0 feature — don't conflate.
- **Veo 3.1** (Google) — the current Google model: native audio by default (always-on via the Gemini API), scene extension, last-frame control, extensions to ~148s. Google AI Plus $7.99/mo (Fast tier) is the most aggressive consumer entry price in the field. API benchmark ~$3.20/8s — the premium API tier (reported, Sept 2026). **CORRECTION (Oct 11, 2026): Veo 4 does not exist.** Pages titled "Veo 4 release date" ranking on Google are **SEO bait** — no Google documentation names such a model (verified across three sources: lumeflow.ai, innfactory.ai). Google's actual next play is **Gemini Omni**, unveiled at Google I/O 2026 (May 19–20) as a unified multimodal creation platform: Omni Flash shipped day one in the Gemini app, YouTube Shorts, and Google Flow, with API since June 30, 2026 (~$0.10/s at 720p, token-billed).
- **Gemini Omni / Omni Flash** (Google) — the conversational video platform Google built instead of a "Veo 4": prompt-plus-reference generation and clip editing across Gemini, Shorts, and Flow.
- **Runway Gen-4.5** — still the current Runway model: **Runway shipped no new model in 2026.** September's news was distribution (its MCP serving other companies' models) and the Sept 30 Summit. 4K with camera control; consumer plans ~$12/$28/mo; API benchmark ~$1.20/10s 720p (reported, Sept 2026). $200M ARR, $350M year-end projection (company-claimed); research pipeline spans creative video, interactive simulation, and humanoid robotics (world models).
- **LTX-2.5** (Lightricks) — released Aug 11, 2026: Fast/Pro variants up to 4K, open weights 22B, multi-shot in one pass. The LTX line is trained on licensed Getty/Shutterstock imagery — the legal-safe open pick for commercial work (paid license required above $10M revenue).
- **Wan 3.0** (Alibaba) — formal release Aug 24, 2026: 2–30s with native audio at **$0.05/s at 480p** (provider list price) — "thirty seconds with audio got cheap; a year ago that length and price did not exist together" (makeinfluencer.ai). Also rated the budget/fast-drafting pick in October field notes (from ~6 credits/shot on aggregator hosts).
- **Vidu S2** — launched Sept 15, 2026: real-time S2-Avatar (interactive character up to 720p) and S2-Editing (changes a live stream as it plays).
- **Mirage Tesseract** (Mirage, formerly Captions) — launched Sept 22, 2026: agent-driven editing and motion-graphics suite with a free local engine. Not a shot generator — it belongs to the edit/post stage.
- **Seedance 2.5** (ByteDance) — third-party field notes report identity holds up to ~30s. Seedance 3.0 is *reported* in third-party indexes but unconfirmed by ByteDance — treat as rumor.
- **MiniMax H3** (alias Hailuo 3.0) — 2K plates, native stereo audio; $9.99/mo entry, $94.99/mo unlimited, API ~$0.045/s (768p). Open weights released Aug 3, 2026 (base checkpoint; hosted Context-IR/Regenerate-2K stages separate). Optimized third-party inference from $0.01/s.
- **FLUX 3 text-to-video** (Black Forest Labs) — ~34 credits/shot on aggregator hosts.

**Native audio is now standard** across Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.5, MiniMax H3, Wan 3.0, and Veo 3.1 (Oct 2026 coverage).

**Adobe's Sept 8 multi-model in-Premiere workbench is the big workflow shift:** announced at IBC 2026, Premiere now embeds five competing models — Firefly, Google Veo, Runway, Kling, Luma — directly in the toolbar, plus in-timeline AI audio/music generation, an After Effects AI assistant, and audio repair tools. The round-trip export loop is over: editors generate B-roll in-timeline from whichever model wins per shot. (TechTimes, Sept 8, 2026)

**The API pricing war, in one table** (REPORTED benchmarks — third-party reported, not vendor-quoted; Sept 2026, via Higgsfield's AI-video API price comparison; verify live before budgeting):

| Model | API cost per 10s 720p (reported) |
|---|---|
| MiniMax H3 | $0.80 |
| Kling 3.0 | $0.84 |
| Luma Ray 3.2 | $0.90 |
| Runway Gen-4.5 | $1.20 |
| Seedance 2.5 | $2.31 |
| Veo 3.1 | $3.20 (per 8s) |

Veo 3.1 sits alone as the premium API tier. Open-model floors keep falling: LTX 2.5 Fast from ~$0.003/s, optimized MiniMax H3 inference from $0.01/s. **Drafting tiers are now a workflow:** Seedance 2.5 Turbo and Gemini Omni Flash at 360p exist for cents-level prompt testing before hero renders. (MakeInfluencer, Oct 2026)

**Model exclusivity is gone.** fal, Replicate, Higgsfield, Protoface, and Krea now carry all frontier models behind one API key — Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.5, Wan 3.0, Veo 3.1, Grok Imagine, Runway Gen-4.5, LTX-2.5 in one place (Protoface, Oct 8, 2026). The same models appear on Pika, Runway, Luma, Higgsfield, and Krea — platforms now compete on price per second, tooling, and character consistency, not the model list. Margins are moving to workflow tooling and inference optimization.

**Open source, October 2026:** Wan 2.2 (Apache 2.0) remains the practical quality benchmark for open-weights video; HunyuanVideo is the open-source consistency standout (temporal identity stability). LTX-2/2.5 trained on licensed Getty/Shutterstock data — legal safety for commercial work. **License traps to flag:** HunyuanVideo excludes EU/UK/SK and caps at 100M MAU; CogVideoX caps free commercial use at 1M visits/mo; LTX requires a paid license above $10M revenue. (intelligibberish.com, Oct 2026; Medium open-source stack guide, June 2026)

**The pricing war cratered generation costs.** 10 seconds of HD video now runs $0.25–$5.00 depending on platform and quality; entry plans start around $8/mo (Pika). Every major proprietary platform restructured pricing since late 2025. Pricing tables differ slightly across sources — these are directional, not quotes.

## Sora is gone

The biggest discontinuation of the year: OpenAI killed Sora. Announced March 24, 2026; the app and sora.com closed April 26, 2026; Microsoft retired Sora inside Microsoft 365 Copilot in late June; the API shut September 24, 2026 with no one-to-one replacement. sora.com now redirects to a shutdown notice with an export button — unexported data faces permanent deletion. The drivers were compute cost and a pivot toward coding tools and business customers; the team moved to world-simulation research for robotics. (gizmodo.com, Oct 2026; versely.studio, Oct 1, 2026)

The guide's model record marks Sora 2/Pro/Max `discontinued` and keeps it for historical reference. **Delete every Sora route from your pipeline** — calls now 410. The migration targets the field roundups recommend: Veo 3.1 Fast, Gemini Omni Flash, or Kling.

## The documented long-form workflow

2026 produced the first real consensus on how long-form AI video (20+ minutes) actually gets made. The documented shape (cinemadrop.com; blog.designhero.tv; a ComfyUI pipeline tutorial, Aug 2026; the MakeMovie open-source project):

1. **Script first, written for short shots.** Human-written script; scenes designed for 10–30s takes — models drift beyond ~15s. A feature is hundreds of takes.
2. **Lock identity at the still stage.** Character/location reference stills (Midjourney, Nano Banana/Gemini, Flux Kontext Dev + PuLID). Iterate on stills: "1 minute on a still saves 10 minutes of re-rendering." **Fix everything at the still-image stage** — stills cost seconds, clips cost minutes.
3. **Shot-by-shot image-to-video.** Approved stills become first frames (e.g., Wan 2.2 I2V 14B, Apache-2.0, ~5s per take); motion prompts describe only what moves. Expect 20–40 generations per shot.
4. **Timeline assembly.** An NLE (DaVinci Resolve/Premiere) or an AI timeline tool — LTX Director 2.0 (MIT-licensed, built on LTX-2.3, with IC-LoRA character consistency, Retake Mode, EditAnything, Audio Inpainting).
5. **Audio in layers.** Music (ACE-Step, Suno, Udio), ambience/SFX (Hunyuan Foley, ElevenLabs), TTS or recorded VO. "A silent AI film is unwatchable" — sound is where production value is perceived.
6. **Upscale and deliver.** Batch 4× upscale (Upscayl, Topaz, ByteDance upscaler); export 1080p high-bitrate MP4.
7. **Cost discipline.** Measure cost per finished minute; lock story → characters → stills before motion; draft cheap, finish expensive; let editing and sound solve problems.

**Continuity is THE bottleneck, not single-shot beauty.** The whole workflow exists to fight drift. And open-source pipelines went production-grade: **MakeMovie** (dreamofxm, Apache-2.0, self-hostable — source audit → script → assets → storyboards → first frames → videos → voice & score → composition → delivery, with human approval gates) is the most complete open reference implementation. (github.com/dreamofxm/makemovie)

## India and Pakistan became unlikely AI-cinema hotspots

The year's most surprising geography:

- ***Sardar Sarvai Papanna*** — Telugu historical animated feature, 145 minutes, "AI-assisted animation and generative computer graphics," theatrical release August 21, 2026, budget ₹3.6 crore. (Wikipedia — flag the exact extent of the AI work as unverified)
- ***The Iskoon Bridge*** — claimed as the first AI-generated Gujarati feature: paranormal thriller based on true events, 82 AI-generated characters, built on the GoSkripto AI platform; teaser unveiled September 25, 2026 in Ahmedabad; theatrical planned November 13, 2026 (Gujarat/Mumbai, then US/UK/Australia/NZ/Canada) plus OTT after. The teaser was NFDC-selected for the AI Impact Summit; human script, dialogue, music, editing, direction. (vninews.com, Sept 25, 2026 — single source, flag)
- ***Ainak Wala Jinn*** — Pakistani AI-generated 3D animated feature, theatrical July 24, 2026, based on the 1990s PTV children's series. The original show's creator, Hafeez Tahir, publicly denounced it — excluded from the production, accused it of degrading the property, cited inconsistent visuals and character models. (pakistanicinema.net, Aug 2, 2026 — single source)
- ***The Next Salahuddin*** — "first Pakistani AI-generated film," cinemas plus HUM TV, January 2026; Jinn TV × Cinta Gaza Malaysia collaboration, on the Palestinian plight. (pakistanicinema.net — single source, flag)

And in the West: ***The Cully Hill Boys*** (110 minutes, August 2026, reportedly made on Higgsfield — single source, flag) and ***NAGIN – Season 1*** (38-minute AI fantasy series on YouTube, 2.16M views as of October 5, 2026 — single source, flag). Every documented case relies on human script, direction, and edit.

## What to watch next

- **Kling 4.0's full launch** — announced, priced only by rumor, specs at leak-level. Don't plan around it until it's GA.
- **Seedance 3.0** — reported in third-party indexes, unconfirmed by ByteDance. Treat as rumor.
- **Veo 4** — does not exist; "Veo 4" pages are SEO bait. Google's play is Gemini Omni (see the correction above).
- **Long-form coherence research** — Google Research's four-system framework (AI Video Co-Director orchestration, CANVAS visual memory, A²RD long-horizon synthesis, VQQA artifact repair) targets coherent minutes-long video — but it's research only, no downloadable product. (AlphaSignal, Sept 2026)
- **Cannes** — Reuters (May 15, 2026): organizers have not banned AI outright; films "primarily driven by generative AI" are excluded from Palme d'Or competition. Cannes 2026 was the first festival where filmmakers openly admitted AI use (Demi Moore / Peter Jackson pragmatic, Seth Rogen opposed, del Toro demanding the generative-vs-assistive distinction); assistive AI is increasingly accepted. The major-festival path for AI-driven films still runs through Tribeca, Venice's orbit, and the dedicated AI festivals — not the Palme d'Or.
- **Costs keep falling; taste keeps mattering.** The field's advice going into Q4: delete dead routes, draft cheap, upscale last, and spend the savings on sound and edit.

## Honest gaps in this snapshot

- 2026 image/audio model launches (ElevenLabs, Suno, Udio version numbers) could not be reliably documented this pass.
- *Critterz* (OpenAI-backed, Vertigo Films + Native Foreign, announced September 2025 for a 2026 theatrical + Cannes bow) — could not verify a 2026 release happened. Unconfirmed.
- Festival prize figures below are reported by press, not audited.

<!-- chapter: craft/story-structure.md -->
# Story Structure for AI Short Films

## The short-film engine

A 3–5 minute AI film needs exactly three things:

1. **One want** — the protagonist wants something concrete, visible on screen
2. **One obstacle** — something specific stands in the way
3. **One turn** — the moment everything changes

Most AI-film losers are tech demos with no second act: pretty shots, no turn. Judges (especially Oscar-caliber ones) punish this first.

## The judged-short template

- **Cold open (0:00–0:30):** drop into the world mid-action. No setup, no title cards explaining the premise.
- **Escalation (0:30–2:30):** the want meets the obstacle, pressure builds. Each shot raises the stakes or deepens the world.
- **Reversal (2:30–3:30):** the turn — the plan fails, the truth lands, the choice gets made.
- **Button (3:30–5:00):** one final image that reframes everything before it. End on the image, not on explanation.

## Writing for the model

Design scenes around what AI renders well; write away from what it doesn't.

**Lean into:** single subjects, strong silhouettes, weather and atmosphere, landscapes, slow deliberate motion, objects and environments, stylized looks.

**Write around:** complex hand action, crowd choreography, intricate dialogue scenes, fast fight choreography, text/signage in frame, real people or voices (festival rules forbid them anyway).

**The constraint is the style:** the best AI films don't hide the medium — they pick stories the medium tells better than live action could (impossible scale, dream logic, metamorphosis).

## Scene design checklist (per scene)

- [ ] One clear want visible in the frame
- [ ] One action per shot, five seconds or less each
- [ ] The turn is a visual event, not dialogue
- [ ] Every scene either raises stakes or deepens world — never both vaguely, never neither
- [ ] The ending image is planned before the first shot is generated

<!-- chapter: craft/cinematic-language.md -->
# Cinematic Language

The shot vocabulary and camera grammar that make AI video read as cinema instead of a screensaver.

## Shot sizes — what each one is for

| Shot | Use |
|---|---|
| Extreme wide | World, scale, isolation |
| Wide | Geography — where the story happens |
| Medium | Action and dialogue — the workhorse |
| Close-up | Emotion, decision, detail |
| Extreme close-up | Texture, eyes, objects that matter |

Festival rule of thumb: earn your close-ups. Wide → medium → close builds pressure; starting close spends it.

## Camera movements — the working lexicon

| Move | Prompt phrasing | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Dolly in / push-in | "camera slowly dollies toward the subject, smooth stabilized movement" | Portraits, reveals, rising tension |
| Dolly out / pull-back | "camera pulls backward, revealing the environment around the subject" | Scale, aftermath, loneliness |
| Pan | "slow camera pan across the scene" | Surveys, transitions between subjects |
| Orbit | "camera orbits around the subject" | Hero moments, product, dance |
| Crane | "camera rises and pulls back, revealing the scene from above" | Endings, scope |
| Handheld | "subtle handheld shake, documentary feel" | Urgency, realism — use sparingly |
| Static | "locked-off static camera" | Dialogue, tension, confidence |

"Slow dolly push-in" beats "zoom in" every time — name the physical move, not the effect.

**Motivated vs unmotivated:** every move must reveal or withhold something. A drifting camera with no purpose is the #1 tell of amateur AI video. If you can't say why the camera moves, lock it off.

## Lighting — write it like a gaffer

Vague lighting gets vague images. Specify direction, quality, and color:

- **Direction:** side light, backlight/rim, top light, underlight
- **Quality:** hard noon sun, soft overcast, flickering torchlight, neon spill
- **Color/temperature:** golden-hour warmth, cold blue night, sodium-orange street
- **Motivation:** every light needs a source in the world — window, lamp, neon sign

Example: "dramatic golden-hour side lighting with long shadows" will always beat "nice lighting."

## Composition

- **Rule of thirds:** place the subject off-center; give the frame somewhere to breathe
- **Depth staging:** foreground, midground, background all doing something — this is what makes AI shots feel expensive
- **Leading lines:** roads, corridors, light beams pulling the eye to the subject
- **Negative space:** emptiness is a compositional choice — isolation, scale, dread
- **Don't overcrowd:** fewer subjects per frame = fewer failure modes

## The "cinematic" recipe

"Cinematic" is not a word you add — it's five things combined:

1. **Camera** — one intentional movement
2. **Subject** — one believable action
3. **Environment** — subtle motion (dust, smoke, cloth, water)
4. **Lighting** — explicit, motivated, consistent
5. **Texture** — film grain, anamorphic cues, shallow depth of field

Example: "Slow cinematic dolly forward toward an ancient temple entrance. Priests walk calmly up stone steps while torch flames flicker. Thin smoke rises into warm evening air. Cloth banners move gently in the breeze. Stable architecture, realistic human motion, dramatic golden-hour lighting."

Note: every movement has a purpose, and the prompt asks for exactly one action per subject.

## Sources
- http://answerbeam.blogspot.com/2026/10/how-to-generate-video-from-image-with.html
- https://github.com/servanter/ai-magic/blob/HEAD/content/blog/best-ai-video-generators-2026-sora-runway-kling-pika-comparison.mdx
- https://medium.com/@gencaycubuk/i-tested-dozens-of-runway-prompts-this-framework-creates-cinematic-ai-videos-every-time-e171658033e1
- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z8IaWHEYfpY

<!-- chapter: craft/character-consistency.md -->
# Character Consistency

The technical discipline of keeping people and worlds stable across shots. This is where most festival entries die.

## The identity stack (ranked by reliability)

1. **Trained identity (Soul ID):** the gold standard. Train once on 20–80 photos; the face holds across every generation. See `higgsfield/soul-id-deep-dive.md`.
2. **Character sheet as reference:** front / 3/4 / side views of the character, used as the reference image whenever drift appears.
3. **Per-generation reference upload:** anchors one generation; drifts across many. Fine for single shots, not films.
4. **Text description alone:** weakest. Never rely on prose to hold a face across 50 shots.

## Wardrobe and props lock

- Write the wardrobe once, in exact language, and paste it verbatim into every prompt: "worn brown leather jacket, white t-shirt, dark jeans, scuffed boots."
- Props get the same treatment: one description, reused exactly.
- If the wardrobe changes mid-film (it should, for story), that's a new locked description — never improvise it per shot.

## World consistency

- **Locations:** generate and approve a master still of each location first. Every shot in that location starts from it or references it.
- **Lighting continuity:** lock time of day and light direction per scene. "Golden-hour side light from frame left" in every prompt of the scene.
- **Era/grade:** pick the era and color palette up front (Higgsfield's era selection helps); don't grade shot-by-shot and hope.

## The chaining discipline

- **Last-frame chaining:** every clip starts from the last frame of the previous approved clip. Never fabricate a start frame.
- **Approved-frame library:** keep every approved still/frame. New shots start from library frames, not fresh generations.
- **Rejection rules:** a clip fails if the face drifts, wardrobe changes, the light flips, or the camera moves without motivation. Failed clips don't chain — they get re-prompted.
- **One human per start frame** (for character-led work): crowded frames multiply failure modes.

## The consistency checklist (before any generation)

- [ ] Identity system chosen and trained (Soul ID for films)
- [ ] Wardrobe description locked, verbatim
- [ ] Location master stills approved
- [ ] Light direction + time of day locked per scene
- [ ] Start frame is real (approved frame or trained identity), never invented

<!-- chapter: craft/directing-performance.md -->
# Directing Performance in AI Video

AI models don't act. They render plausible arrangements of pixels that read as acting when the direction is specific enough — and collapse into mannequin theater when it isn't. This chapter is the directing discipline behind believable AI performance, drawn from productions that solved it in public.

## The core problem

Passport Rush's team documented it openly: **AI struggles with subtle character acting.** The failure has a shape:

- Faces average toward neutral — micro-expressions collapse into a pleasant blank
- Emotion labels ("she looks devastated") produce stock expressions, not felt ones
- Dead, glassy eyes — the single fastest tell of an undirected AI performance
- The Verge's review of Cully Hill Boys noted "occasionally weak character interactions" as a visible limit even at $2M

The fix is not a better model. It's direction written the way actors need it — as *tasks*, not adjectives.

## Direct, don't describe

ONEIRIC's acting skill (`tig-acting-task`) replaced emotion labels with acting tasks entirely. The closing rule of that production: **direct, don't describe** — scene event, motive, goal, obstacle, tactic.

| Instead of (description) | Write (direction) |
|---|---|
| She looks devastated | She is trying not to cry in front of him — jaw set, eyes on the door |
| He is furious | He is deciding whether to hit him — weight shifting forward, hands opening and closing |
| They are in love | She keeps finding reasons to stand closer; he keeps noticing and not moving away |
| He is nervous | He is rehearsing what to say — lips moving silently, thumb rubbing the ring |

Every entry on the right is a *playable tactic* — something a body can do. Models can't render "devastated." They can render a jaw set and eyes fixed on a door.

## Give the eyes a job

The single highest-leverage performance note in the research: **"dead, glassy eyes are never fixed with lighting — they're fixed by giving the eyes a job."**

The CINEDANCE prompt architecture gives GAZE/EYELINES its own block *before* blocking. In practice:

- Name the eyeline target per beat: *Mara holds on Vex's hands until "the ledger" — then snaps to his eyes*
- Eyes move between targets; they never "look sad into the middle distance"
- Avert, hold, search, track — eye verbs are direction, not decoration
- In dialogue coverage, the listener's eyes do half the acting — cut to the listener

If a performance feels dead, check the eyes first. Nine times out of ten there's no eyeline written.

## One feeling per shot

AI can't play an arc inside a single clip. It can hold one tactic for 4–8 seconds. So:

- Break emotional turns into separate shots — the turn happens *in the cut*
- The reaction shot is your best friend: AI renders listening better than it renders complex feeling
- Moment-to-moment tactics tied to dialogue words (the `tig-acting-task` block form): each line gets its own tactic, each tactic its own shot if needed

## The director's read

Before generating a scene, ONEIRIC's pipeline produced a "director's read": **the one shared event every character lives through, plus each character's physical channel for it.** Everyone in the scene is experiencing the same event — but grief lives in Mara's hands, in Vex's jaw, in the kid's feet. Write the event once, then assign each character their channel. This is what keeps ensemble scenes from becoming four mannequins emoting at the camera.

## Casting the face

Consistent identity *reads* as good acting. A face that drifts 5% between shots reads as a bad performance even when the "acting" is fine:

- Lock the face anchor; never re-run the base portrait
- State changes (dirt, wounds, tears) are masked integrations, not re-generations
- For recurring characters, identity systems (Soul ID and equivalents) beat per-prompt description

The audience forgives a limited performance from a consistent face. It never forgives a great "take" from a stranger.

## Ration the close-up

Micro-acting is the weakest link in every current model. Spend close-ups at emotional peaks — that's where the audience looks hardest and where the model fails most visibly. Wides and mediums carry the rest; they read as confident filmmaking anyway.

## Dialogue performance

- Short lines per generation; native-audio quotes for the delivery, not the face
- Let the voice carry the acting — don't ask the face to do what the voice already does
- The listener's reaction shot sells the line more than the speaker's mouth
- For long scenes: generate silent, isolate vocals, post lip-sync — the performance lives in the edit

## Rehearsal is drafts

Treat 720p drafts as rehearsal takes. Watch for: does the tactic read? Do the eyes have a job? Does the turn land in the cut? Re-direct with changed variables — a new tactic, a new eyeline — never the same prompt hoping. Three failed rehearsals means simplify the shot, not the actor.

## When to go hybrid

Some performances AI can't give you yet. The documented answer: put a real human at the emotional core and let AI handle everything around them.

- **Get Me Out**: a real performer captured the emotion; AI re-skinned the world around her
- **Dreams of Violets**: the director voice-acted every role himself, then AI-converted each character's voice — the performance was human, the timbre was synthetic
- **Cully Hill Boys**: licensed likenesses with expressions and kinematics mapped from the performers' own photos and voice audio — the "acting" was anchored in real performers from the start

Rule of thumb: if the scene's entire job is one human feeling something complicated, that's the scene to shoot for real — or to voice for real — and transform with AI.

## Restraint by default

A whisper out-acts a shout most of the time. AI models default to theatrical — eyebrow raises, forced tears, the full soap-opera register. Strip it:

- **Negative constraints:** tell the model what *not* to do ("no eyebrow raises, no wide-eyed gasps, no tears")
- **Emotional subtext instead of stated emotion:** write the situation that *produces* the feeling, not the feeling
- **Environmental cues:** let weather, light, and objects carry mood so the face doesn't have to
- **Under-direct to unlock expression:** deliberately leave the face under-specified and let the model find expressions itself — over-specified faces go rigid
- **Wider framing reads more real:** a pushed-in over-directed close-up exposes every flaw; ration close-ups (above) and keep them minimal when they must carry the scene

## Two roads to dialogue

Every talking character goes down one of two roads:

- **Road A — native audio:** the model generates picture plus synced dialogue in one pass (Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.0/2.5, Kling 3.0). "TTS optimizes the voice. Native video models optimize the *moment*" — footsteps, room tone, the pause before the sentence, expression and mouth generated as one believable moment.
- **Road B — decoupled:** silent clip + separately produced voice + a dedicated lip-sync pass that reshapes only the mouth (Wav2Lip lineage: audio maps to mouth shapes directly, not via phoneme→viseme tables).

**Rule of thumb:** the moment a client or an exact script is involved, take Road B — you own the exact voiceover, can revise lines without re-rendering picture, and keep a clean stem.

**Model picks for dialogue** (Sept 2026 hands-on comparisons; verify live): quiet natural dialogue → Seedance 2.0; longer complete audiovisual scenes → Seedance 2.5; multi-speaker dialogue, languages, explicit voice control → Kling 3.0; cinematic ambience + AV sync → Veo 3.1. Caveat: more capability ≠ more believable acting — some users find Seedance 2.0's restraint more film-like than 2.5's more "performed" emotion. Choose the model like a casting decision.

**Dialogue prompting that works:**
- Veo: write the line in quotes and attribute it — *"The girl looks up and says, 'It's real.'"* Unattributed dialogue gets dropped or given to the wrong character.
- Kling 3.0: assign lines to characters explicitly, control speaking order and delivery, multiple languages per character.
- Native limits are real: clip caps are short (roughly 8–15 seconds depending on model), so longer dialogue is still an edit; Google's own docs flag that natural consistent spoken audio remains in active development and incoherent speech can occur. Plan for it.

## Direct TTS voices through text

ElevenLabs models (v3/v4) have no emotion selector for most models — you direct delivery *through the text itself*:

- Ellipsis for hesitation, dashes for interruptions, capitalization for stress
- Bracketed stage directions: `[whispering]`, `[laughs]`, `[said angrily in a French accent]`; v4 adds natural-language audio descriptors including environmental cues (`[light rain]`, `[door slams]`)
- Settings that change performance: Stability 0.4–0.6 for expressive dialogue (higher = flatter), similarity boost 0.7–0.8 for clones, style exaggeration 0–0.3 for normal dialogue
- Write **performance arcs, not flat tones**: shift intentions across a script (open serious → build insistent → close warm)
- Test a voice on your actual dialogue before committing it to a main character; regenerate broken lines, not whole scripts

## The dead-eyes checklist

The uncanny valley has biological markers — the specific things AI faces fail. Check for them:

1. **Microsaccades** — real eyes make 1–2 involuntary movements per second; the AI "predator stare" is mathematical stillness
2. **The Duchenne smile** — real joy contracts the eye muscles (eye crinkle); the AI "Pan Am smile" moves the mouth only while eyes stay static, reading as deceptive
3. **Fluctuating asymmetry** — real faces are subtly asymmetric; generative models average toward hyper-symmetrical faces that read as artificial
4. **Pupillary response** — static pupils read as "soul blindness"

Practical read: **teach the machine to be flawed to be accepted** — prompt imperfection (asymmetry, blemishes, irregular blinking) or fix it in post. Perfect symmetry is the tell.

## Hybrid, done honestly

The estate-approved precedent: *As Deep as the Grave* recreated Val Kilmer with estate permission (children Mercedes and Jack), SAG-AFTRA guidelines followed, estate compensated, voice from pre-tracheotomy recordings. And the producer's framing is the transferable practice — he stopped short of calling it a Val Kilmer performance: **"Val Kilmer influenced this performance."** Honest framing for synthetic performance is itself a craft standard.

The cautionary case: a synthetic performer's live interview froze and veered into 20 seconds of Cantonese — three outlets corroborated. Synthetic performance fails in public in ways human performance doesn't. Keep synthetic performers inside edited, controlled contexts.

## Take workflows: rehearsal as a department

The AI take pipeline: **Idea → Generation → Iteration → Selection → Direction → Editing.** If everyone can generate, the filmmaker's most valuable skill is direction.

- **Hero frame first:** generate the perfect still, then animate it — cast the take visually before it performs, separating the identity decision from the performance decision
- **Scene Lock:** once a take is approved, lock the performance and re-render the camera around it — the instruction changes from "generate this scene from over her shoulder" to **"photograph this exact performance from over her shoulder."** The model must stop reinterpreting dialogue, gestures, pauses, props, and positions after approval. This is the closest thing AI directing has to "we got it, moving on"
- **Scheduled regeneration, not continuous re-rolling:** the generation-supervision pass happens at a fixed point after the rough cut (ONEIRIC); version logs record "version, what changed, verdict" (Cully: 137 entries). Iteration is a scheduled department, not a standing reaction
- **Credit discipline:** price every stage with re-roll allowances, hold a credit floor until picture lock; if spend passes plan by ~15% pre-lock, stop and re-plan

## The performance checklist

- [ ] Every emotional beat rewritten as a playable tactic
- [ ] Eyelines named per beat — every pair of eyes has a job
- [ ] One tactic per shot; turns happen in the cut
- [ ] Director's read written: shared event + each character's physical channel
- [ ] Close-ups rationed to emotional peaks
- [ ] Identity locked — no drift between "takes"
- [ ] Dialogue: voice carries, face supports, listener sells
- [ ] Restraint pass: negative constraints, subtext, under-directed faces
- [ ] Dead-eyes check: microsaccades, Duchenne, asymmetry, pupils
- [ ] Drafts reviewed as rehearsals, re-directed with changed variables
- [ ] Scene Lock after approval — photograph the performance, don't regenerate it
- [ ] The emotional core scenes assessed honestly: AI or hybrid?
