<!-- chapter: craft/color-grading.md -->
# Color Grading AI Footage

Every AI generation arrives with its own built-in grade — the model's idea of what "cinematic" looks like, baked into the pixels. On a multi-shot production, that's 40 different colorists who never met. The colorist's job on AI footage is **unification**: bringing neighboring shots to one look.

## The two places color lives

**In the plate (before generation).** Lens character, palette direction, texture, time-of-day — baked into the location/character image plates. What you bake, you don't have to fix. The ONEIRIC rule: *the plate itself becomes the lens.*

**In the grade (after generation).** Shot-to-shot matching, the show look, technical delivery. What the plate couldn't hold.

Decide per element which place it lives. Anything the video model keeps dropping belongs in the plate. Anything that needs to move across the whole film belongs in the grade.

## The unification pass

Before any creative grading, unify. Pick one hero shot per scene as the reference. For every other shot:

1. Match exposure and white balance to the reference (scopes, not eyes)
2. Match contrast curve — AI generations vary wildly in black level
3. Match saturation — see the de-plasticize stack below
4. Only then apply the creative look

Do the unification pass over the location set *before* generating where possible (the ADILIADA production did this) — it's cheaper than discovering mismatch in the grade.

## The de-plasticize stack

AI footage has a recognizable syndrome: over-smooth gradients, over-saturated color, waxy skin, a sheen over everything. The fix, in order:

1. **Desaturate 10–20%.** AI oversaturates by default. This one move does half the work.
2. **Add fine film grain.** 35mm grain breaks up the smooth gradients that scream synthetic. Grain is the fastest anti-plastic pass in existence.
3. **Subtle chromatic aberration** at high-contrast edges. Real lenses have flaws; perfect edges read as rendered.
4. **Soften, don't sharpen.** Plastic + sharp = worse. A whisper of diffusion beats any sharpening pass.
5. **Skin last.** Skin is the hardest surface — if it's waxy, a dedicated skin-refinement pass or slight diffusion on skin tones only.

Check the whole stack on a big screen. Defects invisible on a laptop appear at 4K.

## Matching across models

Different models have different "house grades" — Kling's contrast curve isn't Veo's. When a scene mixes models:

- Unify harder: match to the reference before any creative look
- The plate matters more: shared plates across models do more than any grade can
- If two models won't match, re-generate the outlier rather than torturing the grade

## The show look

Once unified, the creative grade. For AI film, restraint wins:

- One look for the film, with scene-level variations — not a new look per scene
- Work in passes: primary (whole image) → secondaries (skin, sky, key objects) → texture (grain, halation, gate weave if period)
- Halation and bloom flatter AI highlights, which tend to clip harshly
- Decide the grain philosophy early: one grain for the film, applied at the end, over everything — it's the final unifier

## Scopes, not eyes

Grade with waveforms and vectorscopes. AI footage lies to eyes — the "cinematic" built-in grade is designed to flatter on first glance. Check:

- Blacks actually reach black (AI loves milky shadows)
- Skin tones sit on the skin-tone line (vectorscope)
- Saturation doesn't clip in any channel

## Delivery

- Festival masters: 16:9 or 21:9 composed (not cropped) for the ratio, up to 4K
- Broadcast-safe levels; -1 dBTP audio ceiling is the sound department's job, but don't crush the picture to compensate
- Keep the pre-grade masters. When the festival asks for a revision, you re-grade — you don't re-generate.

## The grading checklist

- [ ] Look decided per element: plate vs grade
- [ ] Unification pass before creative grading (reference still per scene)
- [ ] De-plasticize stack applied: desat, grain, CA, soften
- [ ] Skin checked on a big screen
- [ ] Multi-model scenes matched or re-generated
- [ ] One show look, scene variations — not a look per scene
- [ ] Scopes verify blacks, skin line, saturation
- [ ] Pre-grade masters archived

## Sources

- ONEIRIC brief: colorist-as-unification, bake-the-look-into-plates (third-party transcription — flagged)
- ADILIADA: pre-generation unification pass over the location set
- Companion: skills `craft-kill-ai-look`, `fix-plasticky-look`, `craft-bake-look`

<!-- chapter: craft/sound-music-audio.md -->
# Sound, Music & Audio

Sound is half the picture. Amateur AI films are silent or slapped together; finished ones are designed. This chapter is the audio pillar: strategy, voice, music, sound design, and the mix.

## The audio strategy: native vs. designed

Some video models generate audio natively with the clip (Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.0, Kling 3.0). Treat native audio as raw material, never as the mix:

- **Keep it** when it's ambient texture: room tone, wind, rain, crowd murmur, footsteps. Native models generate believable "moments" — the pause before a sentence, the room the voice sits in — because picture and sound arrive as one believable event.
- **Strip it** when it's dialogue, music, or anything prominent. Those get built deliberately, on their own tracks, where you control every word and note.
- **Never** let native audio be your only sound layer. It's a bed, not a mix.

The clip caps are short (single-digit to ~15 seconds depending on model), so any dialogue longer than a line or two is an edit anyway. Plan for that from the start.

## Voice design: casting a synthetic voice

A voice is a cast member. Cast it with the same discipline you'd cast an actor:

- **Write a Voice Bible** per character/narrator before generating: register (chest/head), timbre (rough/smooth), tempo (unhurried/clipped), manner (warm, flat, sardonic). Every generation references the same bible — this is what keeps a voice consistent across scenes.
- **Test on your actual dialogue**, not a demo sentence. A voice that sounds great on a demo line can collapse on your character's hardest scene. Test the hardest line first.
- **Generate per paragraph, comp like a session.** Paragraph-level generation gives you edit points; comp the best takes the way a dialogue editor comps a real VO session. Regenerate broken lines, not whole scripts.

### The two roads to a talking character

- **Road A — native:** the model generates picture plus synced dialogue in one pass. Best for short lines, natural delivery, ambient realism.
- **Road B — decoupled:** silent clip + separately produced voice + a dedicated lip-sync pass that reshapes only the mouth. Best the moment a client or an exact script is involved — you own the voiceover, can revise lines without re-rendering picture, and keep a clean stem.

Rule of thumb: if the words must be exact, take Road B. (See the `audio-lip-sync-route` skill for the per-scene decision procedure, and `craft/directing-performance.md` for dialogue performance direction.)

### Directing TTS voices through text

Most TTS models have no emotion selector — you direct delivery through the text itself:

- **Punctuation as direction:** ellipsis for hesitation, capitalization for stress, dashes for interruptions.
- **Bracketed stage directions** on current voice models: `[whispering]`, `[laughs]`, `[said angrily]`, plus environmental cues like `[light rain]` or `[door slams]`.
- **Settings that change performance:** stability around 0.4–0.6 for expressive dialogue (higher goes flatter), similarity boost ~0.7–0.8 for voice clones, style exaggeration low (0–0.3) for normal dialogue.
- **Write performance arcs, not flat tones.** Shift intentions across a script: open serious, build insistent, close warm. A voice that never changes intention sounds synthetic no matter how good the model is.
- **The human-in-the-loop upgrade:** record the acting yourself (even roughly, even on a phone), then AI-convert the voice to the character. The acting survives; the voice matches the cast. This is the highest-quality dialogue pipeline documented in AI film to date.

## AI music: score as a built object

- **Brief per cue, not per film.** Genre, tempo, instrumentation, the cue's emotional job, what to avoid: "ambient synth, 85 BPM, rising tension, no vocals." Generate 3–5 variants per cue and comp sections like a real score.
- **Temp-track discipline:** cut to a temp score first, then generate the final score to the locked cut. Never score to a moving target.
- **Keep stems when the tool offers them.** Dialogue ducks under a full stereo mix badly; stems let the mix breathe.
- **No vocals unless the story needs them.** Score serves the story, never shows off.

### The rights gap (read this before you ship)

AI-generated music sits in the murkiest rights territory in the guide. Model terms vary on who owns outputs, training-data provenance is contested, and distributor policies differ. **Keep your generation receipts** (prompts, dates, tool, terms version) and read `legal/rights-and-disclosure.md` before distributing anything with AI music — especially commercially. This is not legal advice; it's the minimum professional hygiene.

## Sound design & foley: the layer that sells reality

Every scene needs three layers:

1. **Bed:** the ambient tone of the location (room, street, forest, wind) — runs under everything, never drops to digital silence.
2. **Foley:** footsteps, cloth, object handling — the sounds that make movement feel physical. Performed or layered to picture.
3. **Accents:** designed hits for story beats — the turn, the reveal, the button.

AI SFX tools generate all three from text prompts. Describe sounds the way you describe shots: specifically and physically ("gravel footsteps, slow, approaching" beats "walking sounds"). Build backgrounds first, hard FX second, foley third — and use J/L cuts at transitions so no cut ever goes dry. (See the `audio-sfx-bed` skill for the full layering procedure.)

## The mix: balance, loudness, QC

- **Build order:** dialogue first, then SFX bed, then music last. Music before SFX is the classic amateur mistake — build the world, then score it.
- **Dialogue is king.** If a line matters, it sits on top: carve EQ space for it, duck music under it, never let ambience swallow it.
- **Leave headroom.** Peaks below 0 dBFS, dialogue averaging in a consistent band, nothing slamming the limiter. If you're delivering to a platform, check its loudness spec — don't guess.
- **Listen three ways:** headphones, laptop speakers, a phone. If the dialogue survives the phone, the mix works.
- **The silence test:** mute the music. If the scene still plays on dialogue + SFX alone, the design is sound. If it collapses, the music was doing the acting — fix the scene, not the score.

## The audio checklist

- [ ] Ambient bed under every scene — no digital silence
- [ ] Foley on all physical movement
- [ ] Voice Bible written and referenced for every speaking character
- [ ] Dialogue route chosen per scene (native or decoupled — never mixed mid-scene)
- [ ] Score built cue-by-cue to the locked cut, stems kept
- [ ] Generation receipts saved for all AI music and voices
- [ ] Mix QC: dialogue intelligible on laptop speakers and a phone
- [ ] Legal chapter reviewed before distribution (`legal/rights-and-disclosure.md`)

## Sources & confidence

Voice-direction mechanics (bracketed tags, stability/similarity settings, paragraph-level generation) are corroborated across multiple 2026 creator guides; model-specific tag fidelity is vendor-claimed — verify on your tool's current version. The two-roads dialogue framework and native-audio quality markers come from hands-on editorial comparisons checked against official model docs (Sept 2026). The AI-music rights gap is documented in this guide's legal chapter. Clip-cap figures change with model updates — verify live before planning around them.

<!-- chapter: craft/editing-pipeline.md -->
# Editing Pipeline

From selects to festival-ready export.

## Assembly

- **Selects discipline:** generate 2–4 takes per shot, keep the best one. Kill darlings — a beautiful shot that doesn't serve the story is a deleted shot.
- **Cut to the story, not the footage:** the shot list is a plan, not a prison. If a generated shot is better than planned, re-cut around it.
- **Keep ratios honest:** 45–75 shots for a 3–5 minute film. Fewer, better shots beat more, weaker ones.

## Transitions and pacing

- **Cuts over effects.** Hard cuts are invisible; dissolves and wipes announce themselves. Use transitions only when time or place changes.
- **Pacing math:** action sequences cut faster (1–2s shots), emotional beats breathe (4–6s). Vary rhythm deliberately — monotony is the enemy.
- **The J-cut/L-cut:** let audio lead or lag the picture cut. Instant professionalism, costs nothing.

## Color

- **Match AI shots to each other first:** different models and prompts produce different grades. Normalize before styling.
- **One LUT direction for the whole film:** pick the palette in pre-production (era selection helps) and apply consistently.
- **The "expensive" grade:** restrained contrast, skin tones natural, shadows with detail. Over-saturated teal-and-orange reads cheap.
- **Free tools:** CapCut handles LUTs, grain, contrast, and saturation well enough for festival delivery.

## VFX touch-up

- **Cleanup passes:** inpaint glitches, stabilize micro-jitter, remove stray artifacts.
- **Face composite:** plasticky wide-shot faces get replaced with crops from close-shot frames.
- **Grain:** a light film-grain overlay unifies shots from different models — the cheapest consistency tool in post.
- **Upscale last:** finish the edit, then upscale the final timeline — never upscale individual clips and re-edit.

## Delivery

- **Export specs:** match the festival's required format, resolution, and codec exactly.
- **Watermark + packshot:** the Higgsfield festival requires both in the final video — build them into the export, not as an afterthought.
- **Watch it on three screens:** phone, laptop, TV. If it only looks good on one, the grade isn't done.
- **The 24-hour rule:** lock the cut, sleep, watch fresh. Every flaw you catch now is one the jury won't.

## The delivery checklist

- [ ] Picture lock before color and mix
- [ ] Color matched across all shots, one palette
- [ ] Sound mix final (dialogue > score > bed)
- [ ] VFX cleanup pass complete
- [ ] Watermark + packshot embedded
- [ ] Exported to festival spec
- [ ] Watched fresh on multiple screens

<!-- chapter: craft/editing-ai-footage.md -->
# Editing AI Footage

Cutting synthetic footage is a different discipline from cutting camera footage. The material lies to you in specific ways, breaks in specific places, and rewards a specific workflow. This chapter is the deep craft behind the `craft/editing-pipeline.md` checklists: selects discipline for generated takes, how to read AI footage, pacing decisions unique to synthetic material, repair techniques in post, and the regenerate-vs-repair decision that controls your budget.

## The selects workflow

Camera editors log footage. AI editors log *generations* — and the generation carries metadata the footage doesn't show.

- **Keep generation receipts.** For every take you keep, record the model, the prompt (or prompt ID from the workshop), seed if the tool exposes one, and generation date. When a shot needs a re-render three weeks later, the receipt is the difference between matching it and starting over. The workshop's saved prompts (`gallery.html`) are a workable receipt system.
- **Name takes like an editor, not a prompter.** `sc03_sh02_v3_keep.mov` beats `kling_dreamy_final_FINAL2.mp4`. Scene, shot, version, verdict. The verdict suffix (`_keep`, `_alt`, `_fix`) is the whole system — at 2am you should be able to read the selects bin without opening anything.
- **Generate 2–4 takes per shot, keep one.** The failure gallery's lesson applies in the bin: the first generation is a draft. Takes 2–4 are where the model settles. Past 4 takes you're usually prompting the wrong thing — go back to the prompt, not the generate button.
- **The selects bin is sacred.** Only keeps enter the edit. Alts live in a separate bin. This sounds bureaucratic until your timeline has 200 clips and you can't remember which face-morph take was "the good one."

## Reading AI footage: the inspection pass

Before a clip earns a place in the timeline, watch it three times with three different eyes:

1. **The story pass.** Does the shot do its job — the action, the framing, the beat? If not, no amount of clean rendering saves it. Kill it now.
2. **The background scan.** Watch everything *except* the subject: hands at frame edges, background faces, text on signs, architecture lines, reflections. AI failures hide in the periphery — the subject gets the model's attention, the background gets its leftovers. This is where three-eyed cyclopses live.
3. **The motion pass.** Watch at half speed. Look for micro-jitter (the tell-tale AI shimmer on still surfaces), morphing (faces and hands drifting between frames), and motion that "swims" — cloth, water, and hair moving without physical cause. Half-speed reveals what full-speed hides.

**The 5-second rule:** any AI clip held longer than ~5 seconds gets inspected frame-by-frame at its start, middle, and end. Long holds are where drift accumulates past the audience's forgiveness threshold.

## Pacing synthetic footage

AI footage cuts differently from camera footage, for one reason: **synthetic motion has no rest state.** A camera shot of a still room is genuinely still; an AI shot of a still room shimmers, breathes, and drifts at the pixel level. The audience feels this as restlessness even when they can't name it.

- **Cut synthetic footage tighter than you think.** The 2–4 second shot is the sweet spot for AI material — long enough to read, short enough that micro-defects don't accumulate. Camera footage can hold 6–8 seconds on a face; AI footage holding that long invites the audience to study the render instead of the performance.
- **Earn your holds.** When you do hold — an emotional beat, a landscape — make sure the shot earned it in the inspection pass. A held AI shot should be your *cleanest* take, not your most convenient one.
- **Vary rhythm deliberately.** The failure mode of AI editing is metronomic cutting: every shot 3 seconds because every generation came out 3 seconds. Re-time clips. Let some breathe, snap others. Monotony reads as "AI-generated" faster than any artifact does.
- **Transitions are confessions.** A dissolve between two AI shots says "I couldn't make these match." Hard cuts are invisible; every effect announces itself. The one exception: match-cut on motion can *hide* a multitude of sins — cutting on a shared movement vector carries the eye past minor inconsistencies.

## Repair in post: the fix-it ladder

Work the ladder bottom-up. Each rung costs more time than the last; stop at the first rung that works.

1. **Cut around it.** The cheapest fix is editorial: trim the morphing frames, cut before the hand enters frame, use the clean 2 seconds and lose the rest. Most AI defects live at clip heads and tails — the model's "warm-up" and "decay" frames.
2. **Re-time it.** Speed ramps hide jitter: a 90% slow-down smooths micro-shimmer; a slight speed-up tightens mushy motion. Optical-flow re-timing is your friend — it interpolates *between* the model's frames, which often look better than the model's own in-betweens.
3. **Stabilize it.** Micro-jitter on "locked" shots responds well to stabilization with minimal smoothing. Don't over-stabilize — the warp artifacts of aggressive stabilization look worse than the jitter.
4. **Composite the fix.** Plasticky wide-shot face? Replace it with a crop from a close-shot frame, tracked on. Warping background element? Patch it with a clean plate from another take. This is standard VFX thinking applied to AI's specific failure modes.
5. **Grain unifies.** A light film-grain overlay across the whole timeline is the cheapest consistency tool in post — it gives every shot, from every model, a shared texture. Do this *after* the edit is locked, on an adjustment layer.
6. **Upscale last.** Finish the edit, lock picture, *then* upscale the final timeline. Never upscale individual clips and re-edit — you'll pay for pixels you cut.

## Regenerate vs repair: the decision

This is the budget decision that separates professionals from hobbyists. The math:

- **Repair wins** when the fix is under ~30 minutes and the defect is local (a few bad frames, one background element, minor jitter). Your time has a cost, but generation has a cost too — and regeneration is a lottery.
- **Regenerate wins** when the defect is structural (wrong action, wrong composition, identity drift through the whole clip) or when you've already spent 30+ minutes repairing. The doctor (`doctor.html`) diagnoses which failures are structural.
- **The two-strike rule:** if a repair attempt fails twice, regenerate. Repair attempts have diminishing returns; the third attempt at fixing a morph almost never works, and you've now spent more than a fresh generation costs.
- **Never repair what you can re-prompt.** A prompt fix (adding the exclusion block, locking the style bible, simplifying the action) compounds across every future generation. A post fix applies once. When the same defect appears in three takes, the problem is upstream.

## Sound-led editing

AI footage is mute until you give it a voice — which makes sound your most powerful editing tool:

- **Cut to the temp score early.** Even a rough music bed gives synthetic footage a pulse to cut against. Editors who cut AI footage silent tend to cut it metronomically.
- **J-cuts and L-cuts are free professionalism.** Letting audio lead or lag the picture cut costs nothing and instantly makes AI footage feel directed rather than assembled.
- **The mute test.** Mute the timeline: the cut should still play. Unmute: nothing should fight the dialogue. If the film only works with music, the edit isn't done.
- **Foley sells the render.** Footsteps, cloth, room tone — the sounds the model never generated are what convince the ear the image is real. The sound chapter (`craft/sound-music-audio.md`) covers the three-layer build.

## Delivery

- **Match the spec exactly.** Resolution, codec, frame rate, file size — festivals and platforms reject on technicalities without watching a frame. The competition-entry craft chapter covers delivery discipline.
- **Watch the export, all of it, on a different screen than you edited on.** Phone if you edited on a monitor, TV if you edited on a laptop. AI artifacts hide at familiar viewing distances.
- **The 24-hour rule.** Lock the cut, sleep, watch fresh. Every flaw you catch now is one the audience won't forgive later.

## Sources & confidence

The selects discipline and naming conventions are standard editorial craft applied to AI's take economics; the 2–4 takes guidance is corroborated across 2026 creator workflows. The inspection pass (background scan, half-speed motion check) synthesizes the failure gallery's documented defects with standard QC practice. Pacing guidance for synthetic footage is editorial judgment grounded in the uncanny-restlessness observation — treat the 2–4 second sweet spot as a starting rule, not a law. The repair ladder and two-strike rule are shop craft; re-timing and stabilization effectiveness varies by tool — test on your footage. The regenerate-vs-repair framework is original to this guide. No single case study is cited because these are cross-cutting practices, not one film's pipeline.

<!-- chapter: craft/longform-pipelines.md -->
# Long-Form Pipelines: Making AI Films That Survive 90 Minutes

Short films are won with great prompts. Long films are won with *systems*. This chapter is the guide's definitive treatment of how AI features actually get made — synthesized from the productions that shipped 20+ minutes with open, documented pipelines: The Cully Hill Boys (110 min), ONEIRIC (20 min), Passport Rush (hybrid), Hell Grind (95 min), and Dreams of Violets (75 min). Every number carries a source; everything the research couldn't verify is flagged.

## 1. Two ways to build a feature: scene-by-scene vs. sequence assembly

There are two working architectures in the documented record, and they solve different problems.

**Scene-by-scene (the ONEIRIC model).** One scene is developed to completion, then the *next* scene chains off it: each new scene's reference is the previous scene's finished video, not a text description ("a text description drifts over generations — a video reference doesn't"). Per-scene folders hold that scene's assets; the film assembles in script order. This is the continuity-maximal approach: drift is fought at every seam because every seam carries a video anchor. ONEIRIC generated **41,118 assets for ~20 minutes** (~2,050 per finished minute) working this way.

**Sequence assembly (the Cully model).** Nine directors under two leads worked in parallel across ~100 locations, coordinated through a shared canvas system holding sheets, locations, props, and state. Assets were built first (~1,000 production-ready assets in 4K), shots generated in parallel, and continuity was managed by a **137-entry version log** — version, what changed, verdict, per shot. This is the throughput-maximal approach: it needs a team (25–28 people) and a real asset-management discipline, but it finished a 110-minute feature in about four weeks.

**Which to use:** solo or small team → scene-by-scene; the chaining rule is your continuity department. Team of five-plus → sequence assembly, but only if someone owns the registry full-time; without a wrangler, parallel generation produces parallel continuities.

Both architectures share the same foundation: **assets before shots, always.** The working shape is one folder per film — `brief.md` (logline, tools, plan), `script.md`, `registry.md` (named looks + one verbatim descriptor per @-tagged asset), one `shotlist.md` per scene (shot number, seconds, one-line goal, the *entire prompt verbatim*, `look:`, optional `source:`), and a per-shot version log.

## 2. The consistency system: what survives 90 minutes

Three interlocking disciplines, all documented in the open briefs:

**Character bibles.** Two-pass identity locking: a close-up face is generated first (maximum identity detail — the anchor), then full-body looks are built from it. The hard rule: **the base portrait is never re-run through any model.** State changes (scar, haircut, dirt, wound, wardrobe) are integrated point-by-point with masks around the base pixels. Re-running a portrait is how a character "slowly stops being the same person." A state change gets a new @-tag (`@char_ON_Rudy_s2_v1`), never an overwrite — state is an asset.

**Style-locked prompts.** Everything the video model keeps dropping — grade, lens character, texture, time of day — belongs in the *asset image*, not the video prompt. The ONEIRIC team's consistent-lens-look trick: generate the location plate with the anamorphic character baked in; the video model reads the optics off the plate. **The plate itself becomes the lens.** Voice identity is locked the same way: a Voice Bible (register, timbre, tempo, manner) pasted into every generation *verbatim — not even a synonym changed*. Prompts follow a fixed block order (the CINEDANCE order: scene context → references → location map → gaze/eyelines → blocking → timed segments → dialogue → audio → physics → lighting → style → positive locks), and **every prompt is an island**: positions, poses, wardrobe, props, optics, and light spelled out from scratch every time, because "same as the previous shot" is an instruction to a model with no "before."

**Reference discipline.** Video references beat text references at every scale: a Blender previz or the previous scene's finished video is sent as a video reference; a daylight kitchen reference overrules an evening prompt, so *what you want goes in the reference*. For multi-character staging, a color-coded blocking diagram is attached *last* among references (so photos win the style vote), drawn from the camera's side — never a top-down plan ("video models think in frames, not blueprints") — with edits addressed by color ("move the BLUE figure"). Room-heavy scenes add a depth map (black-and-white geometry channel); without it, "a location that rearranges itself every few seconds." Visual anchors — a specific chair, a window characters talk by — are planted and repeated across generations, and the whole location set gets a unification pass (color/light/saturation) *before* generating, which is cheaper than discovering mismatch in the grade.

**An honest note on seeds:** the open briefs do not document seed management as a consistency technique — no production in the research record credits seed-locking for holding identity across scenes. The documented levers are the ones above: locked base pixels, video-reference chaining, and plates that carry the look. Don't build your continuity plan on a lever nobody has published results for.

## 3. Dialogue pipeline at scale: three architectures

Dialogue is where long-form AI films live or die, and the record shows three working approaches:

**Native audio (generate speech with the shot).** Seedance 2.0/2.5 supports native speech in the generation; Cully Hill Boys used Seedance 2.5 for video *and* speech, and ONEIRIC's prompt architecture carries DIALOGUE and AUDIO as separate blocks (audio carries voice identity only). Advantage: lip-sync and performance timing are born together. Cost: every dialogue re-roll regenerates the performance; the Voice Bible must be verbatim every time. Best when: dialogue is sparse or the scene's acting is the point.

**Human-recorded, AI-converted.** Ash Koosha (Dreams of Violets, 75 min) voice-acted *every role himself* at a London studio, then converted each character's voice with AI — ~1,000 audio clips across Resolve and Logic, 35 minutes of original music. Advantage: the performance is directed like a film — timing, breath, emphasis are human decisions; conversion only changes timbre. Cost: you need a recordable voice (yours counts) and the conversion step per character. Best when: dialogue is dense and performance quality is the bottleneck — which, at feature length, it usually is.

**Decoupled (TTS / directed synthetic).** Dialogue generated separately as audio and married in the edit — the approach covered in `craft/directing-performance.md`, with TTS direction (pace, breath marks, emphasis notation) as a writable skill. Advantage: iterate performance without re-rendering picture. Cost: sync and emotional believability are on you; the failure gallery's Tilly Norwood lesson applies — synthetic performers belong in edited contexts, never live. Best when: narration, background voices, or rapid iteration.

**The scale rule:** ONEIRIC's brief is explicit that a one-room dialogue scene held across dozens of shots was the hardest technical task of the film — *harder than the space battle*. Budget your continuity and re-roll effort on ordinary rooms, not spectacle.

## 4. The economics: cost per finished minute, by model

Assumptions, labeled: credit costs from the guide's `models.json` (observed 2026-10-10, Higgsfield pricing page; USD at $0.0392/credit on the Plus plan). "Clean pass" = every second generated exactly once — a fiction in practice; the documented regime is **5–20× regeneration overhead** (tens of thousands of assets per finished minute). Rates move monthly; verify live before budgeting.

| Model (720p-ish tier) | Clean $ / finished min | 20-min film, 5–20× overhead | 90-min film, 5–20× overhead |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kling 2.5 Turbo | ~$1.90 | ~$190–$750 | ~$850–$3,400 |
| Hailuo 02 (768p) | ~$2.35 | ~$235–$940 | ~$1,050–$4,200 |
| Kling 3.0 | ~$3.30 | ~$330–$1,300 | ~$1,500–$5,900 |
| Wan 2.6 | ~$3.30 | ~$330–$1,300 | ~$1,500–$5,900 |

| Veo 3.1 | ~$23.50 | ~$2,350–$9,400 | ~$10,600–$42,300 |
| Seedance 2.5 | rate not in captured table — verify live | — | — |
| Luma Ray 3.2, Pika 2.5 | not in captured table — verify live | — | — |

Cross-check: at Seedance 2.5's API rate of ~$0.0738/s, a 20-minute clean pass is ~$89 and the 5–20× envelope is ~$440–$1,770 — consistent with the table's order of magnitude.

**Why the company productions cost 100× this.** Hell Grind put ~80% of <$500K into compute; Cully Hill Boys put ~$1M (half of ~$2M) into compute. Those are *internal* infrastructure costs at mid-2026 rates for self-run models — plus licensed celebrity likenesses (with contractual biometric-data purges), 15–28-person teams, 4K delivery, and a four-week parallel overshoot. A LinkedIn analysis notes Cully's ~$1M was "a real number for what the production cost at the time it was made" and that rates "are already down since." **Do not quote the $1M figure as a retail budget.** The disciplined retail envelope for a 90-minute AI feature is low thousands to low tens of thousands of dollars — compute is 50–80% of a professional budget, and the scale of waste (re-rolls), not the per-second price, is the real budget line.

Sanity anchors: Koosha's claimed $2,000 GPU total for 75 minutes (his own unaudited first-person figure, with proprietary tooling he says cuts GPU cost 80–90%); single-source trade reporting of $1,000–$3,000 for 20–30-minute AI microdramas (flagged).

## 5. Pacing and structure for AI features

AI features have a specific structural grammar, and the failures are structural before they're technical:

- **Stress-test every scene before generating it.** Goal, Obstacle, Tactic, Reversal, Value Shift — with a verdict and fixes. A weak scene's cost is only discovered *after* it's generated. Then storyboard step-by-step: "only on the storyboard does it become clear how good a scene really is, as opposed to how good it was in your head."
- **Ration your spectacle.** The re-roll budget goes to ordinary rooms, not set pieces. A production that spends its regeneration budget on the space battle and starves the dialogue scenes has the economics backwards.
- **Ration your close-ups.** Close-ups are the identity risk (every pore is a drift surface) and the acting risk (dead eyes at 4K). The dialogue-scene recipe's rule holds at feature scale: close-ups only at emotional peaks.
- **Cut on the dialogue, not the motion.** J-cuts and L-cuts carry scenes across generations better than matched action, because action continuity is exactly what the models are worst at.
- **Post is five stages, and the third one is the discipline.** Assembly → rough cut → **generation supervision** (a scheduled QC/re-generation pass *after* the rough cut — not continuous re-rolling) → fine cut with cold-viewer screenings → picture lock (no new generations except emergencies, with notice to color and sound). The colorist's job is **unification**: every generation ships its own built-in grade.
- **Draft at 720p, upscale winners.** The field-guides' model reference and the budget calculator both encode this; at feature scale it's the difference between a $3,000 and a $30,000 compute bill.

## 6. Honest limits: what still breaks at 20+ minutes

- **The subtle-acting ceiling.** AI struggles with nuanced performance; even at $2M, reviewers flagged "flat, mis-prompted acting" in Cully Hill Boys. Acting direction must be written as eye-work and tactics, never emotion labels — and some performances simply need the human-recorded pipeline (§3).
- **Drift is cumulative, not linear.** Identity and style decay *across scenes*, which is why the chaining rule and the never-re-run-base-portrait rule exist. There is no documented "set it and forget it" consistency setting.
- **The asset math is brutal.** 41,118 assets for 20 minutes. 16,000+ clips for 253 shots. Anyone selling you a feature for the price of the clean pass is selling the fiction.
- **Single-source flags:** Hell Grind's "16,000 clips → 253 final shots" is reported for the first episode (the film may be episodic — don't quote it as a whole-film ratio); its "3,000-word prompts per 15 seconds" comes via a tabloid-grade outlet; Koosha's $2,000 GPU figure is unaudited; NAGIN S1 / Naga Puspa / RAMAM appear in one blog's table only. The guide states these as flagged, not as facts.
- **What the record doesn't contain:** no documented 2024-era long-form AI feature pipelines surfaced — the documented era starts 2025–2026. Techniques from the short-form era don't automatically transfer; the failure gallery exists for a reason.

## The long-form checklist

- [ ] Asset registry complete before shot one: every character, location, prop named, versioned, locked
- [ ] Every scene stress-tested (Goal/Obstacle/Tactic/Reversal/Value Shift) and storyboarded
- [ ] Architecture chosen: scene-by-scene chaining (small team) or sequence assembly with a registry wrangler (team)
- [ ] Dialogue architecture chosen: native, human-recorded + converted, or decoupled — per scene, not per film
- [ ] Blocking diagrams + depth maps for multi-character and room-heavy scenes
- [ ] Base portraits locked and never re-run; state changes = new tagged assets
- [ ] Look baked into plates; video prompts carry only what changes
- [ ] Voice Bible pasted verbatim into every generation
- [ ] Island prompts: everything re-stated, every time
- [ ] 720p drafts; upscale winners only
- [ ] Generation supervision as a scheduled post-rough-cut pass
- [ ] Compute budget with 5–20× overhead, not the clean-pass number
- [ ] Picture lock means no new generations without notice to color and sound

<!-- chapter: craft/episodic-shortform.md -->
# Episodic Short-Form: The AI Mini-Drama Pipeline

The most durable format in AI short-form video right now is not a single short — it is a *series*. Numbered episodes, one emotion each, voice-led, cliffhanger endings, and a caption that is itself the hook. This chapter adapts the genre into a repeatable production pipeline: nine stages, hard budgets, nine quality gates. The craft lesson underneath is old: a serial lives or dies on the bible, the arc, and the cut — AI only changes which of those costs the most money.

## The observed case

The pipeline below was reverse-engineered from the TikTok account **FutureGalaxyStories** (@uq6ctqxxc8), bio *"Creating stories with AI, capturing every moment through visuals"* — 358.8K followers, 6.3M total likes at the time of analysis (Oct 2026). The genre is the AI emotional mini-drama: tearjerker family stories told in numbered episodes — the same genre the `storyreel` skill in the guide's skill library was built from.

The representative episode: **"Episode 3 — A 2-Year-Old Girl Took a Taxi Alone Just to Find Her Daddy"** — 82 seconds, 128K plays, 3,187 likes, 722 saves, 89 shares, 29 comments. The numbers worth studying are not the views; they are the *saves and shares relative to plays* — that ratio is the cliffhanger working. People don't save single jokes. They save things they intend to follow.

*(Episode-pipeline research, Oct 2026 — observed case. Single-source, flag: the platform analytics came from the episode page itself, not an independent audit.)*

## The mini-drama boom — why the format is winning (Oct 2026)

Since this chapter was first written, the genre stopped being a niche observation and became the platform's headline story:

- **TikTok has been promoting episodic series since June 2026**, and mini dramas are now the fastest-growing *new* category on the platform (buytiktokaccount.com — single-source, flag).
- Typing "microdrama" into TikTok search now opens a dedicated **"TikTok Short Drama"** section: vertical 9:16 episodes, 1–3 minutes each. Series like *Reborn After He Chose Her*, *Spoiled by the CEO's Family*, and *My Fluffy Alpha Husband* have accumulated up to **455.7M views per series** (tiktoktiktoktiktok.substack.com, Oct 2026 — single-source).
- Sensor Tower's *State of Short Drama Apps 2026*: short-drama apps passed **850M global downloads in Q1 2026 (+140% YoY)**, with average daily viewing at 25 minutes by April 2026 (+85% vs January 2025) (archyde.com, Sept 2026).
- DoubleVerify (Sept 2026): microdramas are **1–2 minute serialized episodes** built on romance, revenge, and frequent cliffhangers; Omdia puts global 2026 revenue at **$14B** (up from **$11B** in 2025, the US accounting for $1.5B — EIN Presswire, Oct 2026 release, single-source). DoubleVerify also flags brand-suitability risk (adult/violent content in some microdramas) — the guide's revenge-arc lane stays non-graphic.
- In China, PhilSTAR Life (Oct 2026) reports **120,000+ microdramas released between January and March 2026, 95% of them AI-generated** — citing Chinese state media and CNN (flag the sourcing chain); Variety describes the AI short-drama shift as faster, more scalable, lower-threshold production. This is consistent with the earlier ~90% AI-generated figure (Kuhn) — the Chinese market is now majority-synthetic.
- The platforms are building the rails, not just the audience: TikTok's **Drama Center** — introduced at its June 2026 Apps Summit — handles series management, multilingual translation, and revenue sharing for in-app Mini Dramas (Technode, June 2026); TikTok + creator agency Amplify launched **"The Next Episode"**, a program funding creator-led series instead of one-off posts (Metricool 2026 creator timeline).

This is validation, not a trend to chase — the pipeline in this chapter *is* the thing the platforms are now rewarding. Why the format wins, in platform-mechanics terms:

- **Serialization is the follow mechanic, and TikTok tests for it.** TikTok's distribution is interest-graph, not social-graph: every upload is tested against a small audience pool and widened only if early signals clear the gates (Hootsuite, Vamp, fivebbc — all three agree). An episode that ends on a cliffhanger with a numbered next part manufactures the follower the algorithm can't give you: someone who returns unprompted.
- **Watch time + completion rate are the dominant ranking signals.** The three sources agree on the order — watch time/completion first, then rewatches, shares, saves; one marketing study estimates the pair at 40–50% of ranking weight (DMA — single-source, treat as lore). One emotion per episode *is* a completion-rate design: nothing leaks the viewer's attention because there is only one thing to attend to. The genre's 60–150s band at high completion outcompetes shorter, leakier clips (DMA lore: a 60s video at 80% completion beats a 15s clip at 95%).
- **Cliffhangers are built for sends.** On Instagram Reels the #1 ranking signal is **sends per reach** (Mosseri, via virvid.ai / CreatorFlow) — and a cliffhanger is the most sendable thing a video can be: *"you have to see what happens next."*
- **The Oct 1, 2026 Shorts originality update REWARDS this format.** YouTube now prioritizes original content in Shorts recommendations and reduces reach at the *channel level* for accounts that mainly aggregate or re-upload (announced by Creator Liaison Rene Ritchie via Creator Insider video + TeamYouTube post; Social Media Today, Oct 1, 2026). An original serialized series is the exact opposite of a clipping channel. The same gate exists on TikTok, which does not recommend reused or unoriginal content (viral.app, citing TikTok docs, Sept 2026). Everything in the nine stages below produces *original* footage — this pipeline was compliant before the rules changed.

The craft consequence: the deep moat (bible, arc, voice-first cut) is now also the platform moat. AI makes the footage cheap; the serialization makes it distributed.

## The genre anatomy — why the format works

Each of these is a design decision you can steal for any series, on any platform:

- **Numbered serialization is the follow mechanic.** "Episode 3" does more work than any hashtag: it tells a first-time viewer there is an Episode 4, which is the only promise that converts a viewer into a follower. Never post an episode without a number.
- **The caption IS the hook.** The observed formula: `[Episode N] + [one-line emotional stake] + [CTA]`. The caption names a character and a stake legible in one sentence — *"a 2-year-old girl took a taxi alone just to find her daddy"* — parenting, waiting, loss, reunion. These are stakes a stranger understands in two seconds. The first three seconds of picture restate the caption visually: a toddler alone in a taxi looking for her father. Caption and opening shot say the same thing; neither makes the viewer read twice.
- **60–150 seconds, one emotion per episode.** The runtime band is a craft constraint, not a platform setting: one episode carries exactly one emotion (grief, relief, dread — pick one word). Two emotions in 90 seconds reads as noise. The beats structure serves the single emotion: hook line in the first 3 seconds → 3–5 simple beats → a dedicated shot for the emotional turn → the cliffhanger.
- **Voice-led, not music-led.** Narration and dialogue carry the story; there is no reliance on trending audio. This is what makes the genre agent-producible: a locked dialogue track is deterministic, cheap, and version-controllable, where trending-audio strategy is not.
- **Cliffhanger endings, always.** Every episode ends mid-beat or on an unanswered question — never the resolution. The resolution is what Episode N+1 *is*. The craft name for this is the soap-opera pacing beat: gut-punch, then a question or an interrupted line.
- **The funnel CTA.** "More inDrama↓" teases a longer cut on a drama app. That is an external business funnel; the production pipeline produces the TikTok episode itself. Steal the shape (tease the next thing), not the destination.

The deep moat is not the animation — the genre's visuals are slow, simple, character-consistent frames; *the story does the work, not the animation.* The moat is the arc: a locked character bible, per-line voice-first editing, and dialogue-locked cuts. Everything else is execution.

## Four more working serialized formats (Oct 2026)

The mini-drama pipeline above is the flagship, but the boom is wider than one genre. Four more serialized short-form formats are demonstrably working right now. Each follows the same skeleton — numbered episodes, one unit of tension per episode, cliffhanger endings — with a different engine under it. Each entry: the format, why it works, and a fictional worked episode-block example showing the block structure.

### 1. POV micro-series — "you" are the protagonist

**The format.** Second-person scenarios, one per episode, numbered: *"Episode 1 … POV: You insulted a stranger yesterday… and today he's your billionaire boss"* — the "Hallway series" by @quiet.truths742 (76.4K likes, 134 comments on Episode 1; TikTok, Oct 2026). Each episode is a single encounter with one power reversal; the camera is the viewer's eyes.

**Why it works.** The "you" casts the viewer — no character introduction needed, no bible to lock, and the stakes are instant (status, embarrassment, desire). It inherits the mini-drama pacing (gut-punch → reversal → cliffhanger), but the cliffhanger is always social: *what happens when he sees you tomorrow?* The comment section does the distribution work — viewers tag the friend who "would absolutely do this," which is sends-per-reach fuel.

**Worked episode-block example** *(fictional — shows the block structure, not a real series):*

- Format: POV series · Episode 4 · Emotion: **dread**
- Stake: you borrowed your roommate's jacket — the stain won't come out
- Hook visual (first 3s): your hands frantically scrubbing fabric in a bathroom sink, coffee brown spreading
- Beats: (1) the spill, frozen mid-panic; (2) flashback: the roommate lending it this morning — *"take care of it"*; (3) the knock at the door — she's home early; (4) the turn: the designer label — it cost four figures
- Cliffhanger: the bathroom door handle turns — freeze on your face
- Keyframe scenes: sink scrub close-up / flashback handoff / designer label macro / door handle mid-turn

### 2. "Day in the life" AI character vignettes

**The format.** A recurring AI character, 15–60 second episodes from its daily routine — one small event per episode, no multi-episode plot required. An AI-anime creator guide (autoweeb.com, 2026) reports that **short serialized content with a recurring protagonist outperforms one-off images in both completion rate and subscriber conversion**, and that "day in the life" character vignettes work in the 15–60s range.

**Why it works.** The character IS the series — familiarity compounds. Plot overhead is near zero (routine + one surprise), so the nine-stage pipeline runs at its cheapest: the anchor paragraph and voice ID do the heavy lifting, and every episode is four keyframes from one world. The follow mechanic is parasocial, not narrative: viewers return to *see how she's doing*, the way they check a friend's story. The bible is the whole show here — G0 discipline is the quality bar.

**Worked episode-block example** *(fictional):*

- Format: day-in-the-life · Episode 12 · Emotion: **comfort**
- Stake: Rin the night-shift barista makes the 2 AM regular's drink before he orders
- Hook visual (first 3s): espresso machine steaming in a dark shop window, rain on glass
- Beats: (1) rain on the window, empty café; (2) the regular's shadow at the door; (3) the turn: Rin is already steaming the milk — she remembered
- Cliffhanger: he slides a folded note across the counter — freeze before it opens
- Keyframe scenes: rainy window / door shadow / steaming milk close-up / folded note mid-slide

### 3. Revenge / betrayal arcs — the justice ladder

**The format.** A multi-episode revenge plot where each episode delivers one injustice and one retaliatory move: betrayal → discovery → the plan → the takedown → the reveal. OutlierKit's 2026 niche data gives betrayal & revenge storytelling a **21x breakout rate** with $20–$25 CPMs on YouTube (outlierkit.com — creator-reported ranges). In short drama, ReelShort's *Your love is my poison* (60-second episodes of betrayal, hidden identities, second-chance romance — viral early 2026) and Playlet's *Never Betray the Woman Who Built You* (affair reveal in minutes, revenge escalating episode by episode) show the funnel pattern: free episodes as TikTok/Reels clips, the full series behind the drama app — *"Continue the story here 👉🏻 Find the full series on the ReelShort app"* (md-eksperiment.org watch guides, 2026; TikTok promo posts).

**Why it works.** Catharsis is the most portable emotion on the internet: the viewer arrives already angry on the heroine's behalf, so the hook costs nothing. The justice ladder is a natural episode map — each episode is one rung — and the cliffhanger is always *the next move*. Finales get the thesis line (the pipeline's G7 rule), which is why these series convert to the paid funnel: the thesis is the product.

**Craft caution.** DoubleVerify flags that some microdramas carry adult, violent, or criminal content and advises brand-suitability review (Sept 2026). The guide's lane: non-graphic, feel-good vengeance — the betrayal is emotional, the revenge is a comeuppance, never gore. A revenge series with the pipeline's single-emotion discipline reads as empowerment; without it, it reads as slop.

**Worked episode-block example** *(fictional):*

- Format: revenge arc · Episode 6 · Emotion: **triumph**
- Stake: Nadia exposes the business partner who stole her designs — at his own launch event
- Hook visual (first 3s): a runway spotlight swinging onto a garment that is unmistakably hers
- Beats: (1) the crowd gasps at her stolen collection; (2) Nadia in the back row, phone raised, recording; (3) the turn: she live-posts the original sketches — timestamped two years earlier; (4) the audience's phones light up, one by one
- Cliffhanger: the partner spots her in the crowd — freeze on his face
- Keyframe scenes: spotlight garment / back-row recording / timestamped sketches on a phone / his frozen face

### 4. Interactive / comment-driven episodes — the audience votes, the story obeys

**The format.** One decision per episode, and the decision is genuinely handed to the viewers: the episode freezes on the choice, the vote runs natively in the comments, and the *next* episode plays out the winning choice. The comment section becomes part of the writers' room. The vote mechanic is now platform-native: TikTok's comment polls — rolled out globally on Sept 3, 2026 — give creators up to five options, a creator-set timeframe, and real-time results tracked in the comment thread (TechCrunch / USA Today, Sept 2026). The platform's own suggested uses include voting on the next video idea: the interactive format is the serialized form of that exact behavior.

**Why it's verified, not trend-hype.** This is the strongest new sub-format of the cycle, with evidence on both sides of the fence:

- **Interactive production is now a stated product category.** Singapore-based DRAMAGO (an AI-native drama platform) announced Sept 30, 2026 that it has built its catalogue around interactive drama since April 2026 — 14 AI-produced dramas released, 10 of them interactive — and plans a Q4 2026 beta of an "AI Story World" where the audience keeps questioning the story after the episode ends (FinanceWire press release, Sept 30, 2026 — company-claimed).
- **The audience is already doing it on TikTok.** Sydney Robinson's (@thatgirlsydjo) five-part "Group Chat" series — fictional drama unfolding between a group of friends, played by one creator — opened at 30M+ views and 20,000 comments of viewers demanding more episodes (Dexerto). A vertical-micro-drama survey paper (Zenodo, late 2025) documents the behavior explicitly: viewers *roleplay in the comments*, anticipating characters' next moves — "effectively becoming a shared communal experience." Some micro-drama apps have already built in-app discussion threads and polls so viewers vote on plot twists (same paper). TikTok has been adapting too: an experimental "Minis" series section in the main app and, by early 2026, PineDrama as a separate app to organize episodic shorts with continue-watching rails.

**Why it works.** Participation is a stronger follow mechanic than emotion. A cliffhanger asks the viewer to *return*; a vote asks them to *invest* — and investment converts: the voter has to come back to see whether their choice won. The comment section does double duty as distribution (comments are engagement signals) and as the writers' room (the winning vote and the strongest minority theories become episode N+1's block inputs).

**The pipeline rules for this format:**

- **One decision per episode** — the interactive analogue of the two-emotions rule. Two votes splits the comment section and kills the funnel.
- **The decision beat freezes on the choice** — generate a freeze-frame-friendly keyframe with clean composition; do NOT burn the poll into the video. The native comment poll does the asking — it stays editable, tallies itself, and enforces the deadline.
- **The vote gets a real deadline** ("the winning choice plays out tomorrow") — open votes feel like homework; closed votes feel like a game. The comment poll's built-in timeframe *is* the deadline: set it when you post, not in a pinned comment after.
- **The vote wins, always** — rigging or ignoring the result reads instantly in the comments. The format's contract is participation.
- **Harvest the comments** — the winning vote and the loudest minority theories become the next block's stakes, hook, and beats. Log the poll tally from the in-thread results into the arc tracker. TikTok's Sept 2026 comment overhaul made the comments a media surface — voice comments (up to 60s, 18+) and photo comments roll out alongside polls (TechCrunch, Sept 2026) — so the loudest minority theories may arrive as audio: transcribe before harvesting.

**Worked episode-block example** *(fictional):*

- Format: interactive · Episode 3 · Emotion: **suspense**
- Stake: Lena finds a door in her apartment that was not there yesterday
- Hook visual (first 3s): a door where a wall should be, light leaking underneath
- Beats: (1) the impossible door; (2) the vote: she knocks — or walks away (the decision beat, freeze on her hand); (3) she follows the winning choice — the consequence plays out; (4) the turn: what is behind the door reframes the question
- Cliffhanger: the next decision point — freeze before the vote closes
- Keyframe scenes: impossible-door close-up / decision-beat freeze (native poll UI asks — no burned text) / consequence beat / decision-point cliffhanger

*Honesty note on the rest of the cycle:* multi-POV telling (the Group Chat phenomenon is inherently multi-character) is a *technique inside* these formats, not a verified standalone AI format; duet/stitch chains are a 2020-era mechanic, not new; and "ask the AI character" Q&A accounts (e.g. the Eleanor account's "ask AI anything") show no verified Oct-2026 serialized-mini-drama traction — reported as observed, not as a format pick.

## Studio 2.0 — the pipeline's production-planning end

The guide's [Studio](../studio.html) now runs the episode pipeline as a planning tool end to end:

- **Series mode** — plan 3–10 episodes in one pass. Each episode is a full production plan (shot list with per-shot prompts from the 47-template library, per-shot model picks from `models.json` with real cost math, budget lines, schedule), wrapped in a **series bible**: locked cast anchors + locations and a **prompt-DNA block** prepended verbatim to every shot prompt in every episode — the pipeline's official cross-episode consistency engine.
- **The bridge** — "Send series to Studio →" in the [Episode planner](../episode-planner.html) stages the saved series (title, logline, cast anchors, every block's format/runtime/beats) into the Studio, which pre-fills project type (most common block format), episode count (block count, 3–10), per-episode runtime (median beats × seconds-per-beat snapped into the format's band), cast rows, and attaches each block's emotion/beats/hook/turn/cliffhanger as the episode's arc — no skeletons when bridge arcs exist.
- **The production packet** — the deliverable: the full costed packet (bible, per-episode arcs + shot prompts with locked DNA, model picks, budget with the "saved by the bible" reuse line, schedule, the consistency checklist) exported as Markdown or a self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, a print stylesheet, and zero external requests.

**The reference implementation.** A full 5-episode mini-drama — *"The Night Bus"* — runs through this whole chain in `~/workspace/tiktok-episode-pipeline/WORKED-EXAMPLE-5-EPISODE.md`: concept → five planner blocks → the bridge handoff → a Studio series packet with real cost math (50 shots, $20.48 clean / $102.40 at 5× / $409.60 at 20×, seed `b272deb1`), and the nine gates walked for episode 1. The numbers are asserted against the real engine in `scripts/agent-workflows.test.js` (workflow 5) — if the underlying model data changes, the test fails rather than letting the example drift.

**A documented build.** TheWrap's StoReel Canvas experiment (June 2026) is the most honestly documented AI microdrama build: four one-minute episodes in four days for ~$150 of credits — a 50-page script from one prompt (Claude, five minutes), a one-click breakdown into characters + settings + a 146-clip storyboard, 300–400-word stage-direction prompts per 10–15s clip, and paid character regenerations when faces drifted. The pipeline shape matches the nine stages above — and the failures match the skipped stages: the reporter never edited the AI-generated stage directions, so the acting came out wooden and a wall went missing mid-scene. Qidian Interactive's Wuxi studio (Sixth Tone, June 2026) runs the professional version of the same flow: three small groups (characters + settings, generation, edit — one to two people each), a reusable digital prop room, and the industry's "drawing cards" retake discipline (three to five attempts per usable shot). See the full shot-by-shot teardown ([teardown.html](../teardown.html) — "The $150 Microdrama").

All four formats plug into the same planner. The [Episode planner](../episode-planner.html) now has a **format picker** (mini-drama / POV series / day-in-the-life / revenge arc / interactive) that pre-fills the block skeleton per format, plus a **runtime estimator** (beats × seconds-per-beat) that checks the estimate against the genre's runtime band before you save — the dialogue-budget rule, enforced at the planning stage instead of discovered in post.

## The nine stages, adapted

The production pipeline runs one episode at a time inside a series scaffold built once. Per the research artifact:

1. **Series setup (once):** series config (name, hashtag, voices, episode counter), a character bible with one fixed anchor paragraph + one verified reference image + one locked voice *per character*, and the full 3-act arc (8–12 episodes) with a per-episode block for every episode. Cast: 2–4 characters; no new characters mid-episode. *Craft note: the bible is a contract. Redesigning a face mid-series is not iteration — it is a continuity failure the audience reads as a new character.*
2. **Episode prep:** pull the episode block from the arc — one emotion, hook visual for the first 3 seconds, cliffhanger. Write the caption *first*, from the formula, before shooting anything. If the caption for episode 1 isn't clickable, the series isn't ready.
3. **Script:** 8–12 lines of spoken-form dialogue — characters talk *to each other*, no narrator, soap-opera pacing (hook line → banter → gut-punch → cliffhanger question). Spoken-form rules: spell out numbers, no stage directions, no markup. Read it aloud: hook line lands in line 1, last line is a question or an interrupted beat — never a resolution.
4. **Voice first — lock the dialogue track before any image work.** Synthesize the full script for a duration check (8–12 lines ≈ 60–90s; cutting words is free, re-cutting video is not), then synthesize per line, decode to WAV (never concat MP3s — junk leading frames silently eat segments), concat, and verify the total equals the sum of the parts to the frame. Per-line durations *are* the edit map: line boundaries are guaranteed word-gap-safe cut points. No forced alignment needed. First word starts ≤0.3s from t=0 — the genre has no establishing lead-in.
5. **Keyframes:** 3–4 vertical 9:16 stills per episode, each anchored on the locked character reference image plus the anchor paragraph verbatim, scene description, and an explicit no-text-in-frame instruction. Scene plan per episode: (1) hook shot = caption restated visually, (2) beat coverage, (3) the emotional turn's *dedicated* shot, (4) cliffhanger shot. The turn and the cliffhanger each get their own keyframe — never share a shot with the setup. Verify every keyframe before animating: on-model, text-free, 9:16. *Craft note: faces are a one-time decision. A bible character with a real expressive mouth can lip-sync; a locked flat face (dot eyes, stitched smile) must stay still forever, with voice and burned captions carrying the dialogue. Prompting mouth motion on a locked face doesn't add acting — it redesigns the character (pink noses, eyebrows, anime eyes).*

*Tooling note (Oct 2026):* multi-reference video models accept the bible's locked anchor plates directly — Vidu Q4 Preview (launched Oct 7, 2026) takes up to 15 image references and 3 audio references, with launch pricing from $0.014/s (PR Newswire — preview pricing, verify live). Kling 4.0's announced Omni Reference works the same way, but the full model was still not GA as of Oct 11, 2026 (Flash early access only) — use the bible's plates, not a model you don't have.
6. **Animation:** animate each keyframe — slow push-ins and small gestures, never fast or busy motion. Verify a mid-clip frame for every clip before building the episode around it. If footage falls short of the dialogue duration: up to 9% short, apply a uniform `setpts` slowdown (K ≤ 1.09, imperceptible on slow push-ins); more than that, generate a continuation clip — new frames, same scene. Never reuse or rewind a clip; never let one clip cover two non-adjacent lines.
7. **Assembly — the reproducible cut.** Cut the picture *to the voice*: line boundaries from the duration table are the cut points, and every cut must sit in silence (check the waveform ±0.1s). Never cut mid-word. Bed audio at −18dB under dialogue. Captions burned in as phrase-level ASS (explicit 1080×1920 script resolution — SRT burned through libass without it renders at 384×288 and balloons to poster size). Final duration must hug the dialogue track within ±10%.
8. **Caption package:** the hook-title caption — hook line first (never lead with hashtags), the character named every time (new viewers meet them in the caption), one emoji doing emotional work, the tease as the CTA ("part N+1 tomorrow" — finales get the thesis line instead). Posting discipline: watch once on a phone, first frame = hook visual, one episode per day — never dump multiple episodes at once.
9. **Continuity:** append to the episode log (number, title, emotion, hook, cliffhanger, duration, what worked) and add at least one production lesson — story, timing, or production. Increment the episode counter. Bible discipline holds: anchors, ref images, and voice IDs never change mid-series; if a character must evolve, do it between acts, log it as a deliberate revision, and issue a new ref image.

## The golden rule

**Picture is cut TO the locked dialogue track — never the reverse.** The dialogue duration is the episode's budget; the total runtime hugs it within ±10%. This ordering is the entire production advantage: voice is cheap to iterate (cutting words is free) and expensive to waste (re-cutting video is not). Every stage after voice exists to serve the track, not to negotiate with it.

## Hard budgets

| Resource | Limit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Video generations per episode | ≤ 6 clips | Platform caps and focus; trim hard, best 2–4s slice wins |
| Keyframe generations per episode | ≤ 4 stills | Forces the 4-shot scene plan; fewer, better coverage |
| Dialogue start | ≤ 0.3s from t=0 | Genre rule — the hook line IS the opening shot |
| Runtime vs dialogue | ±10% | Edit feels tight; beyond it the cut reads sloppy |
| Uniform picture slowdown | K ≤ 1.09 | Invisible on slow push-ins; beyond that looks smeary |
| Footage usage | ~50–60% of generated | Trim ruthlessly; coverage is not the episode |
| Bed audio | −18dB under dialogue | Dialogue always intelligible; the bed is felt, not heard |
| Captions | Phrase-level, never overlapping | Start = first word − 0.05s, end = last word + 0.25s |

These budgets are genre-plastic in one direction only: you can spend *fewer* videos or *less* runtime. Spending more on any row is how episodes die in post.

## The nine quality gates

Run every episode through all nine before it ships. A gate fails → fix at that stage, never compensate downstream.

- [ ] **G0 — Series lock:** bible has anchor + verified ref image + locked voice per character; arc complete with all episode blocks and cliffhangers.
- [ ] **G2 — Script:** read aloud; hook line in line 1; one emotion; ends mid-beat (question or interrupted line, never a resolution).
- [ ] **G3 — Voice:** `dialogue.wav` duration equals the sum of line durations; total in the 60–150s band; no line exceeds ~12s.
- [ ] **G4 — Keyframes:** on-model, text-free, 9:16; dedicated shots for the emotional turn and the cliffhanger.
- [ ] **G5 — Clips:** every clip's mid-frame verified on-model; total usable footage within −9%/+40% of dialogue; clip count ≤ 6.
- [ ] **G6 — Cut:** 1080×1920; runtime ±10% of dialogue; dialogue starts ≤0.3s; captions burned, phrase-level, legible; the assembly script re-runs cleanly from scratch.
- [ ] **G7 — Caption package:** hook + hashtags + tease; one-episode-per-day cadence respected.
- [ ] **G8 — Continuity:** episode log + lesson appended; episode counter incremented.
- [ ] **G9 — Cross-episode consistency (series gate):** prompt-DNA block byte-identical across every shot prompt of every episode; anchor paragraphs byte-identical to the bible; no new characters mid-episode; recurring props/costumes carried across episodes per the bible. (Run once per season — or whenever the bible changes.)

(Gates are numbered to match the pipeline stages — G1, the per-episode prep check, is absorbed into the episode block itself.)

## Craft judgment: where pipelines break

- **The turn without a shot.** If your script has an emotional turn but your scene plan has no keyframe for it, you will "borrow" a beat shot in the edit and the turn will land flat. Dedicated turn shot, or rewrite the turn into a line that plays on a face you already have.
- **Two emotions, one episode.** The read-aloud test catches it: if the script makes you feel grief *and* relief, it is two episodes stapled together. Split it.
- **Dialogue drift.** The line-boundary table is only trustworthy if the voice IDs never change and the concat is verified to the frame. One skipped verification and every cut downstream is a guess.
- **The bible is a social contract with your audience.** Every mid-series redesign resets the viewer's memory of who your character is — in a genre where the cast is the brand, that is the costliest failure available.
- **The one-prompt temptation.** Text-to-full-story tools now exist inside the platforms themselves: TikTok's Symphony Agent generates complete ad campaigns from a prompt (on Seedance 2.0), and CapCut's Video Studio advertises type-an-idea → multi-scene emotional mini-dramas (Metricool 2026 timeline; a creator post — treat as directional). They are useful for *drafting beats*, but they skip the locked bible, the voice-first cut, and the continuity log — exactly the three things that turn a pile of episodes into a series. Draft with them if you like; ship from the pipeline.
